Marina Herlop ‘s Dja Dja unfolds like a picaresque adventure through an enchanted world, populated by witches, angels, wolves and other less identifiable creatures. There are moments of childlike wonder, encounters with darker forces and sudden changes of scenery. The Catalan composer’s fifth album, following Pripyat (2022) and Nekkuja (2023), is also her most ambitious undertaking: fifteen interconnected pieces loosely following the archetypal hero’s journey. From the outset, it reveals itself as a beguiling treasure trove of an album.

Herlop has described the process of composing Dja Dja as something akin to solving a giant sudoku. In an interview with The Creative Independent , she explained that she wanted to approach the album as a novel rather than a collection of short stories, mapping out its harmonic, rhythmic and instrumental relationships in advance. This intricate planning is reflected in the recurring melodies and vocal phrases that connect seemingly disparate compositions. “Vas volant” and “Siete mares” share the same invented syllables, while the melody of the former resurfaces in “Lilit”. The words of “As meigas”, meanwhile, return in “Bliss”, with their disturbing references to murderous angels.

Although rooted in Herlop’s Catalan background, the album’s linguistic world extends well beyond it. Catalan, Spanish, Galician and other languages appear in the titles, while recognisable lyrics coexist with her characteristic invented vocabulary. In a 2024 interview with Goûte Mes Disques , Herlop spoke of her growing desire to sing in Catalan, concerned that the increasing dominance of English might eventually erase certain expressions from her native language. Yet language in her music is rarely confined to communication. Words and syllables are chosen as much for their phonetic qualities as for their meaning, allowing the voice to become an instrument in its own right.

The opening “Flor de los precipicios” introduces this peculiar world through Herlop’s acrobatic singing and a prominent flute, one of several wind instruments that provide much of the musical scaffolding of the album’s early stages. With “Vas volant”, the adventure gathers momentum, the music taking flight through a succession of buoyant electronic figures and intricately arranged vocal patterns. “ツラ” conjures something resembling an imaginary bioacoustic environment, alive with unfamiliar calls and rustling activity. Elsewhere, the metallic percussion of Balinese gamelan enters Herlop’s increasingly elaborate musical constructions.

As the journey progresses, keyboards and brass acquire greater prominence. “Jaque” introduces a more confrontational atmosphere, its forceful instrumental gestures suggesting a contest of musical wills, while the exuberant “Los dos lobos” pits looping voices against unruly percussion and swaggering brass. The effect is often wonderfully absurd, as though the inhabitants of an elaborate cabinet of curiosities had suddenly sprung to life and begun arguing among themselves.

But the journey also has its moments of defeat. “You’ve Lost Your Muchness”, a title borrowed from the world of Alice in Wonderland , is a brief, disorientating interlude populated by strange, gurgling voices and fleeting electronic apparitions. Herlop has identified it as the album’s lowest point, deliberately removing the comforting familiarity of repetition to create an atmosphere of unease. The gently articulated guitar of “Hay ángeles” then brings the music back to more recognisably human territory, before “Average Evil” stages another lively encounter between competing rhythmic figures and sharply articulated vocal syllables.

“Bliss” erupts into a joyous collision of bass, percussion and vocal acrobatics, culminating in a flurry of synths. But the album refuses to end on such a victorious note. Instead, “Muy heladas” returns to the frozen landscape evoked near the beginning, gradually expanding into solemn, almost liturgical orchestral harmonies. The journey has come full circle, although its destination remains ambiguous.

Adobe’s Eric Snowden on How AI Is Changing the Way Designers Work
AI was everywhere at Adobe MAX. In a conversation with Adobe’s Eric Snowden, I wanted to get specific about where it could actually help designers and what they’d want to keep doing…

Following the dialogue around Adobe MAX online felt very different from being there in person. We saw in real time what the programs could do—and reactions were definitely mixed. On Instagram and Threads, users were ready to cut ties with Adobe due to AI finding it’s way into every program in the creative suite. At MAX, though, it seemed to me that the purpose behind creating entry points for AI was all about creating efficiency for the user. Creativity was and will always be at the forefront of Adobe’s products, so how can they create a narrative that designers will feel better about when it comes to the programs they have used and loved for so many years?

I put that question to Eric Snowden, Adobe’s Senior Vice President of Design. I’d been reading research led by the University of Exeter’s Saeema Ahmed-Kristensen into how people and ChatGPT generate ideas for design tasks. Ahmed-Kristensen found that the model could produce ideas in volume, but its suggestions tended to cluster around similar concepts. I was curious about how Adobe could help designers see where AI was expanding their options and where their own judgment was shaping the work.

Snowden went back to a notable demo previewed at MAX, the grid demo. The designer asks the agent to lay out images or check brand colors while they work on something else in the same document. “You can use AI without ever generating anything,” Snowden said. It makes us think that the purpose of AI is to assist rather than to create.

I thought about how often I’ve gone through a file at the end of a project looking for the one thing I might have missed. Is every artboard using the approved palette? Are the images ready to go to press? Snowden pointed to an InDesign example that checked whether images were print-ready. I could see that being a major plus on a deadline, when the person who designed the piece is also the last person to review it before it goes out.

Adobe’s Disney example was at the other end of the spectrum. Snowden described how Disney uses its archive to build a custom model and iterate within an established visual world. When I asked what that looked like for an independent studio that is not at the magnitude of Disney, or an independent designer, he described a much smaller starting point. A team could bring in a logo, a typeface, and a few colors, then ask the software to flag where a document strays from the palette.

Later in our conversation, Snowden described using an agent in After Effects to rough out an animation. He went into the keyframes and adjusted the movement himself. When he decided the piece should run for 10 seconds instead of 20, he asked the agent to retime it, then went back in to tweak what he didn’t like.

That example gave me a better sense of what Adobe’s approach could mean in practice. Snowden could make a call about the pacing, delegate the work of shifting dozens of layers, and still get into the file to change how a particular moment landed. An editor might being more willing to try out a shorter or riskier cut if finding out whether it works only takes a few minutes in the background. I can also imagine wanting to explore a series of adjustments to the exact moment a title comes in, because a few frames can change how the whole sequence feels.

Productivity came up often at MAX, but Snowden seemed most excited to share what designers could do with the time they get back. A team could use it to try a direction it would ordinarily drop because the deadline is too close. An independent designer could work through another animation pass or show a client an idea that would otherwise stay in the sketchbook. Of course, that time could just as easily go toward producing more versions on a tighter schedule. The software can make either outcome possible.

I left MAX thinking about the distinction Snowden made near the end of our conversation. “It’s now easier than ever to make something above average,” he said. “I don’t think it’s any easier to make something great, frankly.” Which leads us to what we’ve all seen in the AI wild: logos, posters, and menus are executed every day that often seem somewhere above average, but rarely…

As every self-help book will tell you, it's important to practice gratitude, especially in the darkest times. This year, we invited artists, writers, and art workers from our extended community to share what and whom they're thankful for. Seeing Lorna Simpson’s “Wigs” in a study room with my students at the Museum of Modern Art is an experience in the auratic mysteries of the object: its ability to speak, mutely and persistently. Are we looking at an heirloom catalog or a series of specimens, evidence of female choice, or racial fetishization? The ethical dilemma underlying the very notion of collecting haunts museums themselves as institutional repositories of imperial and colonial appetite. Yet, given our current political moment when inconvenient histories are being systemically and institutionally erased, museums also provide spaces for critical remembrance, crucial holders of the past and how that past continues to shape our present. I remain grateful to those museums today who see education and critical analysis as integral parts of their mission.

In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is now available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture. Having started his artistic journey in illustration, he expanded into painting and sculpture around 2019, developing a visual language that combines realism with subtle surrealist elements. Much of his work centres on the natural world, particularly endangered species and the challenges wildlife faces as its environment continues to change. Through carefully constructed compositions, Andrew captures the beauty and presence of animals while drawing attention to their vulnerability and the importance of protecting the world they inhabit.

A defining feature of Andrew’s work is the way he blurs the boundaries between reality and fantasy. His compositions often place familiar elements of nature within imagined settings, creating scenes that feel at once recognizable and otherworldly.

These dreamlike environments allow him to explore the environmental pressures affecting wildlife while also considering the possibility of adaptation and survival. Rather than focusing solely on the loss and uncertainty surrounding endangered species, He introduces subtle moments of hope, imagining a natural world that continues to find ways forward. Through this balance of realism and imagination, he encourages viewers to look more closely at the relationship between humans and the environment, and to consider the role we play in shaping its future.

Joa Vilallonga is a Peruvian American contemporary artist based in Florida. She completed coursework at the Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes in Lima before earning a BFA in Illustration, summa cum laude, from the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York. In 2017, she received FIT’s Antonio López Alumni Grant.

Her practice spans painting, sculpture, and poetry, with figurative portraiture at its core. Through layered surfaces and restrained tonal transitions, she creates a contemplative atmosphere that defines her visual language. Her paintings unfold as an exploration of stillness, perception, and emotional presence. Her work has been presented in group exhibitions in New York, Tokyo, and Tbilisi. She is a member of Unearthed, an invitation-only community for artists working in analogue, handmade media.

Joa Vilallonga’s paintings explore liminal states beyond linear time, opening visual fields where stillness becomes active. Working within contemporary figuration, she approaches portraiture as a psychological landscape. Her figures merge subtly with their surroundings, inhabiting states of silent depth. Rooted in a self-contained feminine presence, they neither seek approval nor resolution; vulnerability and strength coexist without performance.

Natural elements such as water, wind, gravity, and light function as compositional forces. Water plays a central role in her imagery, suggesting fluidity and receptivity. The human form appears permeable, shaped by transitions that soften boundaries and slow perception. Animals and small organic forms act as quiet counterparts, grounding what cannot be directly spoken.
Through restrained composition, muted palettes, and subtle luminosity, she builds contemplative images that invite sustained attention while leaving interpretation open.

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art . In comparison to the artists’ earlier works , the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson , Marshmallow Laser Feast , and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram .

Much like Poliphilo, the lover of many things, Brazilian musician Veridiana Sanchez, recording as Grimório de Abril , has an appetite for the unexpected. Her latest album takes its title from the extraordinary Renaissance romance Hypnerotomachia Poliphili , published anonymously in Venice in 1499 and traditionally attributed to Francesco Colonna. Written in a hybrid language drawing on Italian, Latin and Greek, the book follows Poliphilo through a labyrinth of dreams, fantastical architecture, gardens and erotic allegories in search of his beloved Polia.

Sanchez constructs a similarly improbable musical universe, bringing together different musical traditions, Czech film music, Ukrainian folk melodies and psychedelic electronics. Yet, as she explains in our interview, the album owes as much to the Renaissance revival of Platonism as to Colonna’s book itself. Her interest lies in the collision of apparently incompatible worlds, an approach informed less by Deleuze’s notion of the incompossible , invoked in the liner notes, than by the surrealists’ fascination with unexpected juxtapositions.

The sprawling, twenty-three-minute opener, “The Seagull / Scarborough Fair”, transforms the familiar English ballad, with its roots in the older Scottish tradition, into an expansive landscape of organ, guitar and shifting electronic textures. “The Magical Garden” draws on Luboš Fišer’s soundtrack for Jaromil Jireš’s Valerie and Her Week of Wonders , another dream of gardens, desire and awakening, while “Polia e Polifilo” moves between spectral voices and delicate, almost incantatory instrumental passages.

“O Jardim das Hespérides” opens with a recorded voice responding to an indecipherable request with a curt “Sorry, wrong number”, an amusingly mundane interruption in this otherwise enchanted universe. From there, an imaginary ecosystem takes shape, populated by electronic birdsong, clarinet and drums, alongside instruments that seem to acquire a life of their own. Nothing is quite what it initially seems, and each musical path seems to fork into another.

The closing “A Carpathian Wedding (for Parajanov)” draws on a Ukrainian folk melody used by Myroslav Skoryk in the soundtrack to Sergei Parajanov’s Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors . The film is almost an ethnomusicological documentary in its own right, so thoroughly does it immerse the viewer in Hutsul musical traditions, from the enormous wooden trembita horns and the resonant drymba (jaw harp) to the sopilka flute, tsymbaly (hammered dulcimer) and traditional bagpipes. Parajanov’s extraordinary fusion of ritual, folklore and cinematic invention has inspired other musicians, notably A Hawk and a Hacksaw, whose 2013 album You Have Already Gone to the Other World was conceived as an alternative soundtrack to the film. Sanchez takes a different route, transforming Skoryk’s folk material into something resembling an eccentric medieval procession, as though a company of troubadours had wandered into a Carpathian wedding, at once celebratory and faintly unsettling.

For all its elaborate references, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili is anything but an exercise in scholarly reconstruction. Sanchez admits that she rarely knows where a composition will lead, allowing instruments, accidents and unexpected combinations to determine its course. She also speaks of her desire to coax an organic sound from the computer, an ambition she recognises as ultimately impossible. Perhaps that is precisely what makes the album so engaging. Like the gardens of Poliphilo’s dream, its musical environments are cultivated but never entirely domesticated, with something strange and unruly always threatening to grow beyond their boundaries.
To help me find the way through this musical labyrinth I spoke to Veridiana Sanchez.

I subtitle this “the secret life of shelves and their inhabitants.” During my recent divestiture of acquired design and design-adjacent artifacts, I’ve realized that I’ve created collections of diverse and incongruent things that naturally fit together. One of my prize collections are a mass of figurines that share only thin connective tissue. Included are small busts of some of the world’s questionable individuals. Another is likenesses of famous and anonymous characters who exude curious hypnotic powers. A third category is trade characters or advertising mascots from various capitalist cultures. It has been said we are what we collect. In fact, we collect what we are.

The one thing that all my collections have in common: They fit together on a shelf, and the juxtaposition of unrelated relations gives them a certain magnetic charm. For instance, I collect miniature chairs—some Midcentury Modern, others old fashioned, and still more without any time or period markers whatsoever. I started collecting miniatures (many are doll house props) on an early visit to Paris, where doll house furniture and fixtures are taken very seriously. The small sizes, enhanced by the attention to detail, were affordable and pleasurable.

There has recently been a trend of social media posts about conferences and retail stores selling miniatures of everything imaginable. Minute doll house furniture and teeny electric train station props have become the rage. I have avidly collected mini anything—from food to weapons—as long as they have some personal resonance.

In Barcelona during Christmastime, the markets are filled with miniatures of El Caganer , which means “the defecator,” or one who poops—and is a traditional mascot of the region. Usually, he wears the traditional Catalonian red cap, a white peasant shirt and squats with his pants pulled down, a pile of excrement steaming under his bottom. Enterprising Catalonians have expanded the tradition to include famous and infamous contemporary personages of all kinds, from movie stars to world leaders. a number of years ago I bought dozens to give as stocking stuffers. My fascination, while shared by Barcelona tourists, was not appreciated back in New York. Nonetheless, such minis as these define my wit and serve, on the whole, as character studies for psychoanalytic probing.

Now, owing to personal downsizing, I have to say goodbye to my gang of miniatures. As I am currently in divesting mode (which includes donating books, posters and art works in record number) I have to relinquish even the tiniest of my collectables to a pile of sacrificial stuff. My collected minis don’t add up to a lot, but they’ve added meaning in my worldview and have become a part of who I am.

The images here are the contents of just a few of the many shelves, display boxes and cases that have swollen over the years with acquisitions made from materials as a diverse polystyrene, polyresin, polymer, clay and ceramic ecosystem of novelty nonsense. On this day before Thanksgiving, I give thanks for all the inexplicable joy they’ve provided.

Birds, browser windows and broken connections: inside Gigi Borgese’s drawings
The New York-based artist combines delicate pencil drawings with the nostalgic graphics of the early internet, exploring intimacy and the blurry line between what’s real and what’s…
The New York-based artist combines delicate pencil drawings with the nostalgic graphics of the early internet, exploring intimacy and the blurry line between what’s real and what’s artificial.

A swallow perches on a white plastic garden chair beside a column of blue folder icons, apparently waiting for a download to finish. A pale sky lifted from a computer desktop frames a bird circled in red under the instruction “Enter the following”, and the answer typed in the box below reads “birds :-)”. In her artworks, Gigi Borgese draws every detail by hand, and the gentle humour really rises to the surface once you know where it all comes from.

Growing up in San Jose, California, Gigi describes herself as largely self-taught, having spent much of her life as what she calls “a passive creative”. Between the ages of 14 and 17, she was an influencer on early TikTok, where the objectification she endured and “the feelings of emptiness/futility in that content” pushed her to delete her accounts and commit to art.

She spent a year at West Valley Community College, then moved to New York in 2023 at 19. She now studies for a BFA in Studio Art at the City College of New York, with a minor in Classics, and has won the Adelaide Jablonsky Award (2025) and the Connor Merritt Award (2026). She was also a finalist in the 2026 Astor Place student art competition, and alongside her degree, she works at the Morris Jumel Mansion on public programming, prop recreation and research.

Her subject matter took shape in 2025, when she was 20. Unknown numbers began texting her doctored and AI-generated images of herself, often depicting her as a minor. “I quickly discovered an active Discord group of over 100 men who had been doing this to me for, at the time, five years,” she says. It sent her back to her years as an influencer and to larger questions around human connection online. “I would not wish that on anyone; however, I credit this event for forcing me to figure out what I wanted to say with my art.”

What she wanted to say arrives through birds, apples and flowers, forms she associates with fragility and femininity, which she then “bastardises” with the visual language of the internet. At 18, she saw Sonya Rapoport’s exhibition Force fields at the Minnesota Street Project in San Francisco, and the artist’s continuous-feed computer paper and early ASCII art “resonated with a part of me that had not yet processed the impact that the internet had on me.”

She’s also drawn to Plato’s ideas about reality and representation. “If the physical world is a flawed copy of our internal world, then the internet is a further copied and flawed version of the physical world.” That chain of copies becomes literal in her work, where you see a swallow multiplying into fading outlines, as if copied and pasted; and a pixelated bird hovering over two ordinary swallows on a yellow grid; and a row of halved green apples placed with the caption “Forbidden (What does it feel like?)”.

To build these scenes, she browses dead websites and old web interfaces, then looks at 19th-century scientific illustrations of flowers and birds. “I find similarity in this artificial attempt to capture the essence of something true,” she says. She works like one of those illustrators, “crudely recreating something with influences from digital spaces”, a method that deliberately mirrors the way the men copied her.

Beautiful Bastard (2026), the piece she says she's proudest of, started when she felt stuck in her older work. Using coloured pencil, graphite, and Micron pen on pastel paper, she draws a poppy “plainly” on the left, and beside it looms a “monstrous, saturated, pixelated imitation of its form”, slightly larger and distorted, yet trapped inside a strict grid. “As the replications continue, the form loses its distinction and our experience with the object changes, becoming less sincere,” she explains.

A Kiss for the Love of my Life (2026) is a simpler piece made of coloured pencil, graphite and Micron pen on Strathmore drawing pad paper – it’s also a little quieter and more disturbing, featuring a swallow kissing a blank, expressionless figure who remains perfectly still. The drawing asks what…
Why Camille Walala is transforming a metro station with 30,000 hand-made tiles inspired by basketball

Alley-Oop, the French-born artist’s first permanent public artwork, pays tribute to a basketball legend and an architectural landmark.

If you’ve spent any time in East London, you’ll probably have come across Camille Walala’s work, albeit perhaps unknowingly; from the Dream Come True Building on Old Street to the stretch of Leyton High Street she covered in grids, triangles and stripes.

Now the French-born, London-based artist is bringing her colourful, Memphis-influenced style to the platforms of Flachet–Alain Gilles metro station in Villeurbanne, part of greater Lyon, France, which serves around 5.7 million passengers a year.

Set for completion next Spring, the installation, titled Alley-Oop, has been created from more than 30,000 hand-crafted ceramic tiles. This will be the biggest project of Camille’s career to date. It’s also her first permanent public-realm work, her first major project in her home country and her first large-scale use of ceramic tile as a material.

Like the Memphis Group that inspires so much of her work – an Italian design and architecture group active from 1980 to 1987 – Camille believes the boundaries between art and everyday life should be porous, or even absent altogether, and that our surroundings should actively shape how we feel.

There are also two specific influences on Alley-Oop. Firstly, the title itself comes from the basketball move where one player throws the ball towards the hoop and a teammate catches it in mid-air and scores. And if you’re wondering what that has to do with rail transport, it’s a nod to the station’s namesake, Alain Gilles, who is considered one of the greatest players in the history of French basketball.

The energy of the basketball court can be clearly seen in the tiles themselves, with rebounding forms, repeated shapes and a rhythm that carries along the platform walls and columns. In a quite magical way, stacked, striped blocks and wavy lines seem to bounce off each other as you move through the space.

A second influence on Camille’s work here is architectural. The commune Villeurbanne is home to a striking 1980s building by Swiss postmodern architect Mario Botta, the MLIS (Maison du Livre, de l’Image et du Son), which features stark geometry, horizontal banding and a dramatic central lightwell.
These forms are echoed in Alley-Oop’s 3D-effect tile patterns, while the palette is said to match the vibrancy and confidence of the decade in which Botta’s building appeared.

“This project means a huge amount to me, and not only because it’s in France,” says Camille. “I have spent many years thinking about the role our environments play in shaping our emotions and behaviours, and my work is animated by the belief that art can drive genuine and meaningful change to our social wellbeing.

“People rarely think about how and what an environment like a metro station communicates with us, and they tend to be quite blank, colourless spaces as a result. With Alley-Oop, we have a wonderful opportunity to engage with the public visually and emotionally, turning a transient transport space into a place of discovery, contemplation and interaction.”
Camille has certainly put the hours in, having spent over four years working on the project to date, making it the most complex and ambitious project in the history of her studio.

She won the commission back in 2022 through an international competition run by Sytral Mobilités, the public transport authority for Lyon. Around 300 artists were in the running to upgrade this and three other stations: Foch, République Villeurbanne and Gratte-Ciel.

Since then, she’s been working alongside architects Atelier Martel, Paris-based art production studio Poïèma and engineering consultancy Betrec. The renovation work has been carried out at night, so that the station can remain open during the entire project. They’ll have spent more than nine months on site by the time it’s finished.

Until now, much of Camille’s best-known work has been temporary; Alley-Oop opens a new chapter for the artist. Fired into ceramic tiles and built into the fabric of the station, it’ll be part of daily life for commuters for…
Carling’s new identity is a badge of belonging inspired by its football ties
BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”. In the last decade or…
BrandOpus has refreshed the much-loved lager brand with a football-style crest celebrating its Burton brewing heritage and its mission of “bringing mates together”.

In the last decade or so, it feels like every British brand has tried to link itself with British football. But some have been in the game, so to speak, longer than others. And if you’re looking for authentic ties, you’ll struggle to find a better example than Carling.

For decades now, it’s been in the hands of fans on matchday, and despite the inexorable rise of hipster craft beers, this honest, reliable, easy-drinking, thirst-quenching amber nectar of a drink (can you tell it’s my favourite tipple?) still gets great love from the football crowd today.

That love has long been two-way. Carling’s name has been on cup competitions, club hoardings and more than a few pub chalkboards for as long as I can remember. And in 2026, they’re leaning into that more than ever, with a refreshed identity built around a football-style badge.

Now rolling out now across supermarkets, convenience stores, pubs and bars, the new identity, crafted by BrandOpus, aims to reimagine Carling’s role in modern culture through the language of community, quality and heritage.

At the heart of the refresh is the new badge, which evokes a sense of the crests stitched onto football shirts. The aim was to make drinking Carling feel more like being part of a team. As Paul Taylor, CCO and co-founder at BrandOpus, explains: “The creative strategy was built around Carling’s core brand purpose of bringing mates together, with all design elements crafted to convey moments of connection.

“Long used in football and communities as a symbol of shared identity, pride and connection, the badge is deployed as a visual metaphor for belonging. It reconnects Carling with its roots, while tying it back to the world of football. It makes the brand feel like a club that people are a part of.”
One good way to convey community and belonging visually is through symbols of heritage and history, and the new design is packed with those.

Inside the badge are illustrations of the historic Carling Brewery and the Burton Bridge, framed by sprigs of barley, with “The Carling Brewery” and “Burton-upon-Trent” threaded around the edge, and Carling’s Black Label banner running across the middle.
For good measure, BrandOpus also added the signature of founder and original brewer Thomas Carling to the can and the glass.

The new pint glass builds on the existing design, which BrandOpus previously helped craft as part of their long-running partnership. This version dials up the heritage messaging with the new badge, along with embossed Burton-upon-Trent lettering near the base.

BrandOpus has also developed a wider, flexible brand world that builds on Carling’s long relationship with football, from grassroots clubs to the Emirates FA Cup and the Women’s FA Cup. This includes a set of illustrated murals and out-of-home assets for stadiums and club sites, designed to adapt to each club’s colours and personality.

All this seems like a smart move for a brand that’s been around for a long time and risks being taken for granted. After all, people’s attitudes to both beer and football have changed dramatically over the past decade, and it feels like the sands are constantly shifting: incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s focus on relaxing the drinking laws at football grounds stands testament to that.
Carling needed to respond to both shifts, reasserting its place in a crowded market while strengthening its ties with the game and the communities around it.

As Ryan McLaughlin, brand director for Carling at Molson Coors, puts it: “This is much more than a packaging refresh. As consumer expectations continue to evolve, it’s important that iconic brands evolve too.

“This is the latest step in Carling’s evolution, building on the strengths that have made it the leading core lager brand in Great Britain, while creating a bolder, more contemporary identity for the future.”
There is something strangely archival about Vestigio, the latest album by Peruvian duo DNGDNGDNG (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue). Its rhythms and sonic patterns have an uncanny familiarity…

There is something strangely archival about Vestigio , the latest album by Peruvian duo DNGDNGDNG (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue). Its rhythms and sonic patterns have an uncanny familiarity, as though they belonged to an established musical tradition, yet their origins are difficult to locate precisely. They seem to come from a geographical territory that has yet to be mapped, let alone explored. The artwork by Joseph Melhuish reinforces this impression, depicting mysterious objects that might be archaeological remains of an unknown civilisation, past or future.

The recognisably Peruvian elements of their earlier releases have become harder to identify. As the duo explained in our interview, they are no longer interested in reproducing traditional rhythms but in extracting certain characteristics and rebuilding them in unfamiliar contexts. This is what gives Vestigio its peculiar character: the music feels familiar without quite belonging anywhere. Rhythmic structures drawn from different traditions are dismantled and recombined with influences from deconstructed club and drum and bass. On “Inercia”, fractured beats and abrupt shifts in rhythm create a sense of constant movement, an approach revisited on “Purpúrea”. Clipping, distortion and resonance are integral to the percussion itself, rather than effects added afterwards. The result is an ebullient album whose rhythmic vocabulary seems to have been invented from fragments of several different musical cultures.

There is also a darker side to Vestigio , most explicitly expressed in the closing track, “Noche Obscura”. Its title references the dark night of the soul , a period of spiritual crisis and eventual awakening. The voices declaring “Están matándonos” (They are killing us) and “¡Nunca más!” (Never again) give the piece an unmistakable political significance. As the duo explained, the track reflects their opposition to state violence and oppression, informed by Peru’s political reality but extending to conflicts and human rights abuses elsewhere.

The title Vestigio refers to something that survives a transformation. Here, traces of Peruvian musical traditions remain embedded in the rhythms, but their origins have become almost impossible to identify. What makes the album so intriguing is precisely this tension between recognition and disorientation: the sense of hearing something familiar while being unable to say exactly where it comes from.
Photo by Alejandro Loayza Grisi : Masks by Tween Muizen
To learn more, we reached out to Felipe and Rafael.

Vestigio is described as your most radical sonic departure to date, with familiar elements of your music broken apart and reconstructed. How did this transformation come about, and what traces of your earlier work, from Zenit & Nadir to Fiebre and Agita2 , do you recognise in the new album?

I think Agita2 was something of a precursor to Vestigio . It was already pointing toward the sonic direction we wanted to explore on the album. Maybe not every track, but several of them contain some of that essence.
There’s also something of the darkness of Fiebre , certain percussive elements, and some connections to Zenit & Nadir . I think the album contains a little bit of each of our previous records.

The idea was to take specific elements from our music, break them apart, and reconstruct them in a different context. Not necessarily to bring back a sound exactly as it was, but to transform it and take it somewhere else.

At the same time, we wanted to push the energy and intensity of those elements much further. I think that combination of deconstruction, reconstruction, and the search for greater intensity is one of the main ideas behind Vestigio .

In earlier interviews, you spoke enthusiastically about Afro-Peruvian polyrhythms and the possibilities of combining live percussion with electronics. On Vestigio , rhythm seems to emerge from the interaction of distortion, clipping and resonance, often becoming jagged and unstable. How has your approach to rhythm and sound design evolved, and what role do traditional Peruvian musical forms still play in your compositions?

Join PRINT Book Club hosts Debbie Millman and Steven Heller for an illuminating conversation with Seymour Chwast , one of the most distinctive and influential voices in American graphic design. A designer, illustrator, image-maker, and visual provocateur, Chwast has spent a remarkable career challenging conventions and expanding the language of graphic communication.

Celebrating two significant new publications, this special event offers an opportunity to explore the thinking, experimentation, and creative sensibility behind an extraordinary body of work—and to hear directly from the artist himself.
Two books. A lifetime of visual invention.
The Picture Book Book: The Art of Seymour Chwast

Created with Steven Heller, this volume explores Chwast’s enduring fascination with the picture book as a medium for storytelling, visual wit, and formal experimentation. Discover an inventive approach to children’s literature that treats the page as a space for unexpected narratives, ingenious imagery, and boundless possibility.

An expansive retrospective of a singular creative life, this landmark volume surveys Chwast’s contributions to posters, typography, illustration, animation, book jackets, woodcuts, graphic novels, and social and political graphics. Developed in close collaboration with Chwast, it brings together personal reflections, previously unpublished imagery, and an extraordinary range of work that reveals the consistency of his curiosity and the breadth of his visual imagination.

Chwast’s work is more than a record of graphic design history, it is a testament to the power of an individual visual language—one shaped by curiosity, humor, experimentation, and an enduring willingness to question convention.

For designers, illustrators, educators, students, and anyone interested in the evolution of visual culture, this is a rare opportunity to consider what makes a creative voice distinctive, how ideas evolve across a lifetime, and why original thinking continues to matter.
Expect an engaging exchange of ideas, insights into the creative process, and a closer look at the work and thinking of an extraordinary design original.

Steven Denekas is a self-taught designer who worked his way from behind the color copier at Kinko’s to now the Head of Design for a product and innovation studio called Siberia . I grew up dreaming of being a musician who toured the world. What is the first memory you have of being creative?

In elementary school, thanks to my incredibly picky palate, my mom packed my lunch every day: a peanut butter and grape jelly sandwich, a bag of Cheetos, and a single Hostess Ho Ho. But that was the feeling. My child was 4 when I started there and 10 when I left. My focus was solely on doing a good job at work, nothing else. I lost six valuable years of watching my child grow up because I was either in the office, at home obsessing over something I did or didn’t do, or just thinking about work nonstop. I was never fully present at home. It took a toll on so many parts of my life, but more than anything, I deeply regret letting my job take priority over my wonderful child during their formative years.

When your heart hurts, you have to hold it and honor the feelings running through your mind. Heartache is a signal that you need to meet the moment with intention. The Daily Heller: A Birds-eye View of a Divided World
An eagle, a dove, and the world today.

The MESS International Theatre Festival is an annual performing arts event held in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Founded in 1960, it is the longest-running such festival. Bojan Hadžihalilović, a creative director and co-founder of Design TRIO Sarajevo and the ad agency Fabrika, has been creating the posters and visual identity for MESS for almost three decades.

More than a stage for performances, MESS is a space for free thought, radical ideas and creative risk. It brings the energy of international theater into dialogue with a region where questions of identity, memory and belonging remain deeply personal.

Its spirit is outspoken, anti-war and firmly committed to human rights, solidarity and peace. It champions artists who confront injustice, challenge authority and give voice to those pushed to the margins. It is a reminder that theater can be both an act of resistance and a gesture of hope—a place where freedom is not simply discussed. Hadžihalilović ‘s recent MESS poster, made from torn and cut paper, is proof of the cautionary and provoking work that is common to his oeuvre. I asked hin to discuss his inspiration and motivation for the struggle between two very clear and recognizable symbols, and how he decided to bring them to life through animation.
What inspired your design of this poster?

The first idea came from how divided the world feels today. Everything seems to be cast in opposites, from yin and yang to dark and light, evil and good, black swan and white swan. That was what made me want to give this divide a visual form.
I kept coming back to two familiar symbols, the eagle and the dove. I liked the idea that you could make both birds from the same material.
It’s in the style of Japanese cutting paper, or origami. A few folds can make a sheet of paper look threatening or vulnerable.
That felt right for MESS, a theater festival in Sarajevo where questions of war and peace have a particular resonance.
Did you see the animation in your mind’s eye before executing it, or during the process?

I’m an old-school designer. I still like to start by picturing a poster in a vertical format, 100 × 70 centimeters. There’s a mantra you hear these days, “The poster is dead!” I always add, “Long live the poster!” Today we call that first image the Q-Visual, the image from which the rest of the campaign grows.
My colleagues at Fabrika took the original poster and built a story from it. The poster gains movement, drama, story and sound and becomes another form of storytelling.
How would you describe the kinetic strength of the image?

For me, it’s all in the tension of that split second before the two birds clash. The eagle seems to be swooping down on the dove to snatch the olive branch from its beak. The poster holds them there, in midair, and the viewer plays out what happens next.
That suspended moment feels very much like the one we’re living through. A dangerous game is playing out before our eyes, all over the world, and the outcome is still up in the air.
What are the emotions that you feel when you experience the image?

I found the whole process of developing the concept for the MESS poster exciting. In the beginning, I was leafing through 50-year-old issues of design magazines like IDEA , GRAPHIC and PRINT , while also exploring what AI could do as I looked for the strongest way to make the image work in black and white.
In the end, I kept coming back to the style and work of my design heroes, Shigeo Fukuda, Ikko Tanaka, Milton Glaser, Saul Bass, Boris Bućan and Mirko Ilić.

You know, I’m from Sarajevo. My city lived under siege for more than a thousand days, facing a ruthless force that seemed ten times stronger. In the end, the people of Sarajevo defended their city, and for a moment it felt as though justice had prevailed. I know it may sound pathetic, but I still want to believe that good wins in the end.
How has the image been received?

It was interesting to see that a poster can still spark people’s curiosity. An image you pass on the street can be a visual provocation, something you keep thinking about and want to talk over with someone else.
Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
The artist's new exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us.

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs , draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel , the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website .

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium.

Model and artist dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram .
Susitse: Fearless journeys into the heart of the beast
Susitse's lifelong interest in canids was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression.
Exclusive interview with Susitse, 3rd Prize Winner, INPRNT Digital Art Award in the 2026 Beautiful Bizarre Art Prize

Susitse’s lifelong interest in canids didn’t just push the Finnish illustrator, comic artist and graphic designer also known as Essi Välimäki to refine her creative skills. Ιt was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression. Her striking, colour-saturated illustrations look straight into the mouth of the beast and expose its heart — inner demons, low self-esteem, toxic relationships, overthinking, grief. A life spent on autopilot.

A time of mental health struggles and targeted self-reflection drove Susitse to find an outlet and seek out people on social media that would help her feel less alone with her emotions, sharing personal messages wrapped in feral snarls of creativity.

Susitse’s surreal, spectacular beasts have human features that convey a touching vulnerability, paired with insightful writing that gives voice to troubled souls everywhere. In her creations, horror and savage comics intertwine with the fragility of human expression, her very real life challenges transforming into dark fables of discovery and self-acceptance. They are lessons in survival and hope exploding in colour — ferocious reds, fantastical purples and luminous yellows.

A daily routine dictated by an employer is, in fact, what inspired Susitse’s prize-winning, poignantly resonant work, Autopilot , kicking back against the idea that we are only meant to be useful cogs in a machine. Playfully dotted with analogue imagery, a multi-headed wolf growls with the age-old fear that our value is limited to performance and production. It is a downright liberating achievement coming from Susitse’s current place as a full-time working artist; a captivating, deeply resonant howl for freedom.
You’ve touched a chord with people online through your illustrations and writing. Does this kind of honest expression come naturally to you, or is it something you have to work on?

Yes, my artistic work has managed to touch people’s hearts all around the world, and I am deeply grateful and humbled to have been able to help people through my art. Open expression comes naturally to me, and it’s reflected both in my art and in my life. I believe that even difficult emotions should not be something to hide or feel ashamed of. Emotions, whether positive or negative, all exist as equals.
“I believe that even difficult emotions should not be something to hide or feel ashamed of. Emotions, whether positive or negative, all exist as equals.”
What’s the process you follow from conception to completion? Is it always a new emotion that sparks an artwork?

Most of the time, yes, at least at the conceptual level! I keep a personal notebook where I immediately write down ideas for a piece that has been sparked by a particular emotion. However, since my art is deeply rooted in emotion, I find that I need to be in a particular “mood” to work on a piece or bring it to completion. This is why I have many unfinished works, as ideas come to me faster than I can actually execute them!

That said, every piece begins with an idea, followed by a quick sketch to plan the composition and colour palette. Next comes the line art phase, followed by base colouring, where the piece receives its initial foundation colours. After that, I determine the direction of the light source and proceed to add shadows and highlights. Finally, if the piece is more comic-like, I add speech bubbles or other text to the piece, and as a very last step, I write a story to support the work.

The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered .
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location , saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch.
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

In court filings and a recently unveiled website , the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security . Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week , Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

Greetings from a Berlin square, where an artist's statue watches over children at play
Children frolic around the ever-watchful and calm Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze, in a square named after the German artist, whose work often depicted children in the wake of World War I.

If you were listening to this, you'd hear what isn't pictured: the whoops and wails of children playing on the swings and slides behind me, all under the watchful eye of Käthe Kollwitz cast in bronze. The German expressionist lived just off this square in Berlin — named after her, Kollwitzplatz — and, at the turn of the 20th century, her children probably played here, too.

In the wake of World War I, Kollwitz's lithographs, woodcuts and sculptures fixated on the suffering and futility of war. They depict undernourished, wide-eyed children in the protective arms of mothers whose anguish is etched into their faces. Her statue, The Grieving Parents , stands in Belgium where her son Peter died at the front, aged 18.

As I turn my back briefly on the playground and aim my camera at Kollwitz, a boy jumps into the shot, up onto the statue's plinth. Playing hide and seek, he conceals himself behind Kollwitz. His friend finds him quickly and the two boys chase each other around the statue, inadvertently embracing Kollwitz like she does her own boys in her lithograph renderings .

The Kollwitz statue's presence is calm. She sits, charcoal in hand, poised to draw the happy hubbub of children growing up in a city that is safe. But with wars not so far away and Germany bringing back military service for a new generation, I feel a sudden urge to wrap my arms around my own child, just as Kollwitz did .

A Van Gogh painting sold for a record $190.4 million Wednesday. But the road to the historic sale was anything but straightforward.

Exhibition of Nazi-looted art asks, 'To Whom Do These Works Belong?

A Vincent van Gogh painting alive with blues, yellows and greens smashed expectations Wednesday, selling for $190.4 million at Sotheby's in New York — more than $10 million above its estimate and an auction record for the Dutch artist. But behind the historic sale lies a darker story of Nazi persecution in the 1930s.

The painting, Châtaigniers en Fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees in English), was painted in 1890 and once belonged to Samuel and Hedwig Fischer, a German Jewish couple. Samuel Fischer founded a publishing company whose authors included Thomas Mann and Hermann Hesse.

The family sold the painting through an Amsterdam gallery in 1936, after Nazi persecution disrupted its publishing business. The auction is going ahead after the current owners reached a last-minute agreement with the Fischers' descendants, who say the painting was sold under financial strain caused by Nazi persecution.

Christopher A. Marinello, a lawyer who recovers lost and stolen art and the founder of Art Recovery International, told Morning Edition such claims can be harder to prove than cases involving artworks seized outright by the Nazis.
"They're a little bit harder to prove, but they certainly carry the same amount of weight," Marinello said.

He described an art market reluctant to confront its past, recalling a client who had to travel to Switzerland after World War II to buy back his own artwork. Marinello also described encounters with dealers who believed the original owners had died.
"Oh, we thought you were dead," he recalled dealers saying.
"They wanted the Holocaust cases to go away," Marinello said.
Sotheby's declined to disclose the agreement's terms, citing confidentiality.
Speaking with NPR's A Martínez, Marinello discussed Nazi-era forced sales, the challenges of restitution and why the art market is still reckoning with Holocaust losses eight decades later.

OUTSIDE IN: New Exhibition at GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester
What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? OUTSIDE IN brings internationally recognised street artists to GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester, exploring…

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction , packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court .

No Regrets: The Mafia connections of Edith Piaf
There’s an argument to be made that in the world of early pop music , Edith Piaf is the French equivalent of Frank Sinatra.

It sounds strange on the surface. Piaf’s regal, haunted demeanour and quiet strength are a contrast to Sinatra’s knowingly sleazy razzle-dazzle, but the deeper you get, the more connections you can find. For one thing, part of what made Sinatra’s Rat Pack persona so compelling was the fact that it covered up a profoundly sad soul. One that, when allowed into the forefront, would make records like In The Wee Small Hours of the Morning and Watertown , albums as classic as they are utterly devastating that could easily have come from PIaf’s soul and been just as affecting.

The big similarity comes in the kind of environments they grew up in, though that’s absolutely not to say their upbringings were the same at all. Much is made of Sinatra’s rough-and-tumble, working-class upbringing in New Jersey, but he lived like a king compared to Edith Piaf. Ol’ Blue Eyes was the only son of two parents who doted on him and made sure he had everything he needed and a lot of what he wanted. Edith Piaf was abandoned as a baby by her mother, grew up in a brothel run by her grandmother , and by 14 was on her own, singing on the streets to survive.

While Sinatra grew up in the orbit of criminals, lowlifes and mafia wise guys, Piaf was raised by them. She was the one who could make it out of the Paris Milieu and, like Sinatra, could lift all boats with her rising tide. No one could see this as clearly as Louis Leplée, an owner of a Paris cabaret who spotted the young Piaf and saw an era-defining star. He took her in, gave her a slot on his cabaret, Le Gerny’s, and gave her the nickname she’d carry her entire life. La Môme Piaf, or The Little Sparrow.

Piaf had finally found someone who really saw something in her and was giving her an opportunity rather than trying to exploit her the way that pretty much everyone in her life had done up until that point. Months later, he was dead. In April 1936, four men broke into his apartment, shot him dead and robbed him of 20,000 francs. Piaf was in Cannes at the time and was inconsolable when she first heard of Leplée’s death. If that wasn’t bad enough, the other shoe dropped soon afterwards.
She was arrested as an accomplice to his murder.

A police investigation had uncovered that a few of the suspects of Leplée’s murder had ties to the same criminal underworld that Piaf had grown up in. The kind that didn’t recognise any honour amongst thieves and would happily extort anyone with cash to spend, no matter if they were friend, foe or family. However, the cabaret promoter wasn’t exactly squeaky-clean himself. There were numerous people who wanted him dead and it was clear that one of the very few people who really, really didn’t was Piaf herself.

She was released without charge, but the whole sorry affair had done serious damage to her burgeoning reputation, people seeing her as a gangster’s moll and not one of the most commanding and compelling singers of her age. This whole affair caused her to take real control of her life, though. She had already begun working with the lyricist Raymond Asso on a few of her early numbers, and in an attempt to cut all ties with her upbringing, she rebuilt her image from scratch under his guidance.

Which is the fundamental difference between Sinatra and Edith Piaf in the end. Frank was a dilettante who got the money and power to get a bunch of crooks on his payroll, and was lucky enough that they stayed loyal to him while coasting on the clout that his mafia connections got him . Piaf was legit. You can tell because her mafia connections did what they do for most people with any actual underworld connections.
They nearly ruined her life before it even got going.
Love at a Standstill — Italian Cold Wave Quartet Winter Severity Index Returns With Video for “Motionless”
I knew you’re there Watching all my movements in the dark. I tried to call your name, But never reached the twinkling in your eyes.
Watching all my movements in the dark.
But never reached the twinkling in your eyes.

Love can make a spectacular fool of anybody with a functioning nervous system. You spend months, sometimes years, investing somebody with qualities they demonstrated on perhaps three occasions, sustaining yourself on the emotional equivalent of a handful of loose change. By the time you realize the relationship has become a private enterprise, with yourself as its sole employee, you’ve practically forgotten what life was like before you started working there. Simona Ferrucci sings from somewhere within this dreadful predicament on Motionless, the first single from Winter Severity Index’s fifteenth-anniversary album, The Brightest Days .

The Italian outfit marks the occasion by reuniting its original lineup: Ferrucci on vocals and guitar, Diana Salzo on bass, Valeria Tirabassi on drums, and Valentina Fanigliulo on synthesizers. Together, the four musicians revisit nine compositions from their formative years, reconsidering arrangements with the benefit of fifteen years spent developing their respective musical sensibilities.

Motionless makes a formidable argument for getting the old gang together. Salzo’s bass possesses that wonderfully oppressive physical presence familiar to anyone who has spent considerable portions of their adolescence listening to Faith and Pornography . Tirabassi establishes a relentless rhythmic foundation beneath guitars that dissolve into great, overlapping sheets of distortion, while Fanigliulo’s synthesizers introduce an almost celestial dimension to the proceedings. Somewhere between the desolate grandeur of early Cocteau Twins and the enveloping guitar treatments of Slowdive, Ferrucci finds sufficient room for her remarkably expressive voice.

There is tremendous emotional friction between the music’s gathering momentum and Ferrucci’s admission of romantic paralysis. Her delivery conveys the exhaustion of someone who has spent too much time negotiating with her own better judgment. As the instrumentation swells, the difficult business of accepting a lover’s indifference assumes almost orchestral proportions. Anyone who has ever mistaken emotional endurance for devotion should recognize the terrible predicament at its center.

Directed by Ferrucci herself, the accompanying video is a beautiful, surreal meditation in black and white, taking us to the seaside and through a series of enigmatic ceremonial gestures. The vastness of the coastal landscape lends a sense of solitude to the proceedings, while the dreamlike imagery gives physical expression to the emotional turmoil within the song. There is something quietly devastating about setting a song concerned with emotional paralysis against the perpetual movement of the sea, suggesting a world that continues along its course while we struggle to extricate ourselves from the past.

Five of the album’s nine compositions originally appeared on the band’s self-produced, eponymous 2011 CDR. The remaining four, The Brightest Days, No Will, Bianca, and Embracing the Void, appeared in different arrangements on 2014’s Slanting Ray , released through Blood Rock Records and Manic Depression Records.

Fifteen years can radically alter one’s relationship with a song, particularly when the people responsible for its existence have accumulated an entirely new assortment of experiences.
