Romance would be considerably easier to negotiate if everybody involved were issued a written itinerary, complete with scheduled moments of affection, designated hours for emotional catastrophes, and a little box to tick whenever somebody felt sufficiently attractive to be loved. Instead, we spend an obscene portion of our existence trying to decipher the intentions of people whose greatest accomplishment might be looking sensational in eyeliner. Fortunately, Astari Nite have a healthy appreciation for the absurdity of these transactions.

On Why Are You So Lame , from Medications In Bloom , Astari Nite indulge their fascination with the psychological misdemeanors of beautiful people, feeding romantic exasperation through the electrical apparatus of industrial rock and glam decadence.

Illia Tulloch’s arrangement possesses the nervous disposition of early Nine Inch Nails, back when Trent Reznor was still figuring out how much machinery he could cram into a pop song before somebody called an electrician. The guitars bristle with distortion, the rhythms twitch with impatience, and Mychael Ghost delivers his grievances with the delicious insolence of a disenchanted teenage idol. Somewhere between the pharmaceutical hysteria of Placebo, the theatrical liberties of David Bowie, and the bruised romanticism of The Smashing Pumpkins, Astari Nite finds ample room for their peculiar personality.

Ghost approaches beauty, rejection, magazine fantasies, and emotional negligence with an almost conversational irreverence. His affection for life’s ridiculous little complications gives the song its character, particularly when desire and disappointment become practically indistinguishable.
“The song is about my truth and friendship with people that I love,” says Mychael Ghost. “Time well spent with others. Engaging without fear.”

Such sentiments extend naturally from Astari Nite’s longstanding fascination with mental health, sexuality, love, and the occult. Their fondness for the alternative rock of the nineties also recalls an era when flamboyance and psychological disarray could coexist quite comfortably within the confines of a three-minute pop song.
The accompanying video embraces spontaneity, transforming a spell of backstage boredom into an impromptu excursion through the peculiar surroundings of a concert venue.

“The video…was captured rather quickly!” says Ghost. “Killing some time, about fourteen minutes’ worth, the band and I were able to film on my telephone. We had just finished sound-checking at a concert we were performing at and were greeted with maximum boredom moments after. So, we found ourselves wandering inside a unique, antique-like venue, roaming freely without a care in the world. What happened next was simply beautiful. I found myself in a land of make-believe, far away from home – lost, curious, and morbidly happy!”

The metal singer who hired a hitman to kill his wife in 2013
Despite the name, in the early 2000s, As I Lay Dying were one of the bigger acts in Christian metal .

This isn’t to say that their entire act was some squeaky-clean, church-approved ‘Christian Rock’ act who led on-stage prayers and were essentially a gospel act with more mosh pits. However, the band made no secret that their music and their lives were informed by the word of Christ and were as likely to be seen on mainstream Christian Rock tours as they were on Ozzfest.

For a period of time, they straddled both worlds pretty well. Heavy enough for the Kerrang! set while legit enough to be the kind of metal band an otherwise concerned Christian parent to think is, broadly speaking, a good influence on their metalhead kid.
Which is some weapons-grade irony, right there.

The band was the brainchild of singer Tim Lambesis, who seemed like something of a metal saint in the years after As I Lay Dying were formed in 2000. His band rocked; he was a legit metalhead covered in tattoos, but he was happily married to his wife Meghan Murphy and had adopted three kids from Ethiopia with her. During the 2000s, the band were a solid mid-afternoon mainstay at Download, comfortably filling rock clubs and small theatres across the world at a time when that could just about sustain a five-piece band and their families. It was a good life. To those outside of it.

In 2012, everything began to fall apart. At first, it didn’t look like it would be all that bad. Of course, a divorce with three kids involved is always rough, but this is rock ‘n’ roll. It happens. Then the actual details of the divorce began to be spread by Murphy herself, and they were not great. Lambesis had lost his faith a long time ago but was keeping up appearances for his career. He was a serial adulterer and, worst of all, his passion for bodybuilding had gotten him into steroids, making him erratic, ill-tempered and occasionally violent.

Their divorce went through and then suddenly, it got much, much worse. On May 7th, 2013, Tim Lambesis was arrested while shopping near his home in Oceanside, California and the story that came from this was more horrifying than anyone could have possibly believed. A month earlier, Lambesis had been idly chatting with a personal trainer while at his local gym before he asked if he knew anyone who could kill his wife. Now, if this was a sick joke, then that would still be cause for concern, but Lambesis was entirely serious.

Thankfully, the personal trainer was disturbed enough by Lambesis’ question to contact the San Diego Sheriff’s Office, which organised a sting operation. On May 7th, a Sheriff’s detective posing as a hitman named “Red” met Lambesis at a branch of Barnes & Noble. Wearing a wire, the detective negotiated a $20,000 payment, which Lambesis paid $1,000 of up front. In the moment of truth, the detective clarified with Lambesis one more time that he wanted Murphy dead. He said, “Yes, I do.”

At first, Lambesis’ legal team entered a not guilty plea on grounds of his steroid use impairing his judgment. However, Lambesis then changed his plea to guilty on one felony count of solicitation of murder, for which he was sentenced to six years in state prison in May 2014. He served four and was released on parole in 2018. Here is where one of the most depressing parts of this hugely depressing story comes out. Lambesis immediately reformed As I Lay Dying with its classic lineup, who all stood by Lambesis’ after he was found guilty of attempting to pay for a woman’s murder.

Six years later, the band fell apart again due to the rest of its members finding Lambesis’ behaviour to them and his new wife abusive and unhealthy. If only there was some way they could have seen that coming.

Blood with blood never made any sense

There is an obscene convenience about the way human beings have learned to manufacture fresh grievances out of old wounds. Somebody gets killed, somebody builds a monument, somebody delivers a speech about the sanctity of human life, and before the flowers have wilted, somebody else is being fitted for a coffin. We’ve become frighteningly adept at compartmentalizing compassion, distributing it according to geographical boundaries and inherited allegiances. Even the dead are expected to carry passports.

Berlin-based singer-songwriter Boris Kaplunovich takes a considerable emotional inventory of this madness in Let It Hurt, the second single from his forthcoming debut EP, due in December. Born in Belarus and raised in Israel, Kaplunovich approaches the subject with the perspective of somebody for whom the notion of home has never been a particularly simple proposition. His experiences of geographical and emotional displacement inform a songwriting sensibility preoccupied with memory, belonging, and the increasingly difficult business of recognizing ourselves in other people.

Kaplunovich confronts the hypocrisy of protecting our own suffering while perpetuating the same horrors against others. Through images of wartime devastation, the lyrics examine collective denial, inherited hatred, and the futility of vengeance. Ultimately, he advocates dismantling tribal divisions, recognizing our shared humanity, and accepting pain as a means of fostering empathy, reconciliation, and healing rather than further bloodshed.

Working somewhere between the biblical bruising of Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, the gothic intimacies of Chelsea Wolfe, and the exposed emotional nerve endings of Emma Ruth Rundle, Kaplunovich draws upon acoustic instrumentation, electronics, and the darker possibilities of post-punk. A multi-instrumentalist who builds his recordings from the ground up, he makes use of the tension between intimacy and enormity, between the private anguish of an individual and the collective sickness of a society that has institutionalized its suffering.

Let It Hurt suggests that pain might constitute a common language rather than another justification for segregation. It takes an odd kind of courage to advocate compassion when anger offers such immediate gratification. There’s a particularly devastating moral proposition at the song’s climax: vengeance cannot deliver justice, and purchasing your own peace with somebody else’s misery is a terrible bargain. The difficulty, of course, lies in accepting this when every institution around you seems determined to persuade you otherwise.

The accompanying video introduces a dark figure whose presence poses an uncomfortable question: are we witnessing somebody mourning the violent deaths of loved ones, or are we looking at hatred itself? Kaplunovich intends the figure to embody both, an unsettling acknowledgment of how readily legitimate grief can be recruited into the service of further atrocities.
Watch the video for Let It Hurt below:

Having shared stages with Micah P. Hinson and Matt Elliott, Kaplunovich belongs to a tradition of songwriters willing to investigate the less flattering aspects of our emotional lives. Here, he asks something considerably more demanding of us than sympathy for the afflicted: the recognition that somebody we have been instructed to despise might be suffering in precisely the same way we are. Imagine the trouble that simple admission could cause for the machinery of war.

‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Strange Town Hides a Terrifying Secret in Paolo Strippoli’s Morality Chiller
A newcomer seeking a fresh start in a town harboring disturbing skeletons in its closet is a well-worn horror setup that Italian filmmaker Paolo Strippoli twists further in The Holy Boy. .

A newcomer seeking a fresh start in a town harboring disturbing skeletons in its closet is a well-worn horror setup t hat Italian filmmaker Paolo Strippoli twists further in The Holy Boy . The slow-simmering morality chiller carefully peels the curtain back on Remis, an isolated town known among residents as the “ Valley of Smiles. ” Behind those smiles, of course, lies a harrowing truth: trauma and pain are vital to the human experience.

Former judo champion turned teacher Sergio Rossetti ( Michele Riondino ) arrives in Remis with the type of severe emotional baggage that makes him a great candidate for the town’s particular type of healing. He’s embittered and still reeling from a profound loss, making him also prone to violent drunken outbursts, which also makes him an early disruptor to the calm status quo. When his latest disruption prompts bartender Michela ( Romana Maggiora Vergano ) to subject him to Remis’ unique form of coping , Sergio finds himself entrenched in the town’s obsession over introverted teen Matteo Corbin ( Giulio Feltri ), whose embrace can erase those pesky feelings of grief and pain.

Though framed through The Holy Boy ‘s audience proxy, Sergio, Strippoli’s third feature is instead more of a grim coming-of-age tale. Strippoli, who co-writes the script with Jacopo Del Giudice and Milo Tissone , slowly unfurls the various traumas that have shaped the town into its current landscape of control, religious fervor, and meticulous maintenance of cheer. At the center of it all is 15-year-old Mateo, a browbeaten introvert trapped in a demanding schedule by overbearing dad Mauro ( Paolo Pierobon ) and the church, there to serve the town and absorb their unwanted emotions. But Mateo has wants and feelings of his own amidst a town of adults that worship him as a saint and peers his age that openly display their resentment.

It’s Mateo, the town’s grim history, and the moral ramifications of the town elders’ choices that are most engaging; The Holy Boy tends to falter and stagnate whenever it attempts to focus on Sergio’s far less interesting trauma. Riondino plays his prickly character with enough defensive guards, save for temperamental crashouts, that it can be tough to fully align with his actions and choices . When the reveal behind his raw pain finally arrives, it’s affecting but thematically far shallower than The Holy Boy ‘s far richer and more nuanced examinations of devotion, obligation, and identity.

Strippoli is also perhaps a bit too measured in keeping Remis’ secrets as concealed as possible until its powerful, shocking conclusion. As such, pacing can sag when The Holy Boy languishes on Sergio too long. While an effective foil, Sergio ultimately feels more of a pawn than a protagonist and is never as interesting as Remis’ peculiar residents.

The refusal to live with suffering dooms a town to a life of artificial happiness, played to chilling effect as its central holy figure, a teen boy longing for normalcy when an outsider shakes up the status quo. Mateo is gifted in more ways than one, but The Holy Boy is at its best when it allows its players to really grapple with whether Mateo’s gift is really a curse, and if controlling such a power can transform angels into devils. Not all of the individual pieces work , but as a whole, Strippoli’s knotted web of morality and identity presents an affecting and potent cautionary tale of human gods and monsters.
The Holy Boy makes its debut on Shudder on November 27 .

The street gang who changed hip-hop by stealing Ralph Lauren clothes
When it comes down to it, pretty much all of fashion , from hip-hop to punk to haute couture, is just status symbols. Few things prove this like Ralph Lauren.

Because their duds show that the very concept of a status symbol is more than just something that looks valuable. Your average polo shirt, after all, doesn’t. Not the way that a tailored suit or a Rolex does anyway. It’s a simple cut, more often than not with one colour to it, one that was originally meant to be practical enough to play a sport in. Weirdly enough, the sport in question was actually tennis; the polo branding came later. To those not in the know, nothing about wearing one would allude to them being a member of the one per cent, so it’s a good thing no one not in the know can afford to be around them.

Because to wear a Ralph Lauren Polo shirt is to exude the feeling that not only are you wealthy enough to afford one, but that alone is enough to make you comfortable in yourself. You don’t need ostentatious designs to show that you’re worthy; you just are. It’s the difference between taste and class and it’s the reason that they were first associated with upper-class preppy kids in the 1970s and 1980s, why do you think the writers of Friends had Rachel working there by the end of the series? One would assume that looks like that would be anathema to the harsh, gritty hip-hop culture of the 1990s, but not quite.

After all, hip-hop is inherently aspirational . The hip-hop story is taking the experiences of a rough, working-class upbringing and using them to create a better life for yourself and your family. What could possibly be a sign that hip-hop was bringing people from the streets into the upper crust than a number of people associated with the culture taking the very image of WASP-ish, rarefied luxury and turning it into something else?

It wasn’t just rappers customising Ralph Lauren fits for themselves, though; it was actual people on the streets who were coming by these clothes in less-than-legal fashion. How did they get them? They got them courtesy of the Lo Lifes, a street gang whose chief operation was heading out from their turf in Brooklyn to upscale Ralph Lauren boutiques in Manhattan and purloining their wares to distribute among the people. It was a huge operation, one that actually came about by two rival gangs putting aside their differences.

The Lo Lifes began as an agreement between Brownsville’s Polo U.S.A and Crown Heights’ Ralphie’s Kids. Former rivals who were both trying to bring the kind of fashion common in Manhattan to the streets of Brooklyn decided that, rather than fighting to try and be the only game in town, it was better to team up and try it together. Taking the name Lo Lifes (the “Lo” in their name being a shortened version of Polo), the gangs found that their strength lay in being together and ended up changing hip-hop fashion forever.

There’s an argument to be made that they created the very concept of hip-hop as high fashion. Up until then, hip-hop stars had been decked out in street clothes of the time (or at the very least had been styled in them by their PR team). After the Lo Lifes began selling high fashion items to their neighbourhoods, and the people they were selling to put their own spin on them, the two worlds collided in a way that they hadn’t before.

The road to rappers walking catwalks and Yung Thug appearing on the cover of his 2016 mixtape Jeffery began with those two gangs putting their differences aside, and there’s something truly beautiful about that.

How Paul Schrader Turned ‘Cat People’ Into One of Horror’s Wildest Remakes
The leap from RKO Radio Pictures circa 1940 to Paul Schrader in the 1980s is like chasing store-brand vanilla ice cream with Cold Stone’s Cat in the Hat’s Cotton Candy Catastrophe. That’s…

The leap from RKO Radio Pictures circa 1940 to Paul Schrader in the 1980s is like chasing store-brand vanilla ice cream with Cold Stone’s Cat in the Hat’s Cotton Candy Catastrophe. That’s not to label old-school Hollywood as drab and droll, but rather to emphasize Schrader’s hold-on-to-your-butts creativity. Jacques Tourneur ’s Cat People (1942) is a black-and-white romantic thriller that coyly teases a domestic nightmare about animalian transformations, but it’s prim and proper for the times .
That’s the glory of early cinema: filmic simplicity, where storytelling has nowhere to hide.

Generational time-jumps like The Blob or The Fly have become seminal examples of horror remakes that justify their way-later revamps; Cat People (1982) deserves similar praise. It’s a shame that David Bowie ’s “ Cat People (Putting Out Fire) ” theme song might be more popular than the film outside genre circles, although fair game, because that was me at one point.

Universal Pictures wasn’t afraid to greenlight a sexually explicit werecat flick for the masses, albeit a harder sell than Poltergeist , Halloween III: Season of the Witch , and other genre titles released the same year.
The 1980s were strange times, and it doesn’t get much stranger than Cat People.

DeWitt Bodeen ’s New Yorker fantasy script bathes in the gender-role stickiness of 1940s cinema, as a magnificent time capsule of martini lunches and wedding bell normalcy. Writer Alan Ormsby ’s many-years-later update couldn’t be further removed, taking the free-spirited erotic route to creature-feature ferocity. Both films are about forbidden lust and sexual consequences, and yet Schrader oversees a far zanier and bolder version. Tourneur thickens tension with questions about whether there’s supernatural mystery afoot. In contrast, Schrader’s first sequence reveals an offworld realm where people are tethered to feline excellence—one grounded, the other gonzo.

German actress Nastassja Kinski stars as Irena Gallier, once orphaned and now a beautiful virgin visiting her brother Paul ( Malcolm McDowell ) in New Orleans for the first time. She learns, ever so awkwardly, that her and Pual’s lineage ties to a community of black leopard worshippers who pass souls through big-cat bodies, and that’s hardly Irena’s wildest discovery. After Irena strikes a hot-and-heavy relationship with New Orleans zoo curator Oliver Yates ( John Heard ), Paul confesses that any intimate extracurriculars will turn Irena into her murderous animal equivalent. The only safe option would be to inbreed, but Irena won’t comply. Thus kickstarts Irena’s adventure through New Orleans: a confused shapeshifter who doesn’t want to kill, yet craves all the same carnal pleasures of regular humans.

Schrader sheds the Pleasantville-era blueprints of 1942’s Cat People for a freakier, fetishistic take on primality. Bodeen pokes and prods Simone Simon ’s Irena Dubrovna from a male-dominated perspective, yet holds back the jungle inspirations of jet-black jaguars kept behind iron bars for a last-second reveal. Ormsby’s horror-centric collaborations with Bob Clark and Joe Dante make sense, given how his Cat People invokes werewolf comparisons, dispelling any concerns that surreality will be held for the third act. Paul wastes no time assuring audiences that 1982’s Cat People wants to platform its Species -like mindset—pre- Species , of course.

It’s not only a magnificent film, but a magnificent remake as well. Kinski’s Irena is freed from her original villain label, embracing the more liberated ideologies of the 1980s, which led to McDowell’s fantastic casting as an antagonistic Paul. There’s no desire to reuse Bodeen’s outdated societal dynamics or Tourneur’s traditional cinematic style. Schrader leans into the gothic haunts of New Orleans while famously aiming for “ more skin than blood, ” turning it into a sweaty, panting address of sinful pleasures.

Why Oliver Reed Was One of Horror’s Greatest Scream Kings
The arrival of Ken Russell’s uncut version of The Devils (1971) in theaters this year has not only kindled interest in the films of the director but also in the work of the film’s star…

The arrival of Ken Russell ’s uncut version of The Devils (1971) in theaters this year has not only kindled interest in the films of the director but also in the work of the film’s star, Oliver Reed .

One of England’s legendary hell-raisers , Reed rose to fame at Hammer Studios , England’s House of Horrors, in the early 1960s. As his star rose, he continued to return to the horror genre, sometimes out of necessity perhaps, but also because of the lure of the material, making him one of the greatest Scream Kings of his generation.

Though not conventionally handsome in the Carey Grant, Paul Newman mold, Reed had an undeniable charisma and animal magnetism that positively erupted from the screen, making his film appearances, from brief cameos to leading roles, indelible and unforgettable.

Reed had landed a few bit roles in the late 1950s, but his career did not really get rolling until Hammer came calling at the end of the decade. In 1959, Reed was invited by one of Hammer’s casting directors, Stuart Lyons , to audition for the studio , and he was eventually cast in a small role in The Two Faces of Dr. Jekyll (1960). He appears in one scene as a bouncer and delivers a couple of lines before being subdued in a would-be barroom brawl by Christopher Lee and Paul Massie .

Still, his work on the film garnered the attention and praise of director Terrence Fisher , who around this time said, “Were I invited to predict sure stardom for an unknown young actor of today, and asked to back that prediction with a heavy bet, the youngster I’d pick would be 22-year-old Mr. Reed.”

Reed won his first leading role over seventeen other young hopefuls to play Leon in Curse of the Werewolf (1961). Though not a hit at the time, the film has become a classic of Hammer horror and the werewolf subgenre. Reed gives a performance of nuance and pathos , expressing the torment of his split nature. Where he truly excels, however, is in his performance as the werewolf, which gives him an opportunity to showcase his remarkable physical presence and abilities. In a way, it was something of an omen for his career and personal life to come . Many have joked that his first big role was as a werewolf and then he went on to become one in real life as his drinking and macho persona became more grandiose.

Another early role was in Captain Clegg , aka Night Creatures (1962), in which he plays the male half of the romantic subplot. The film is odd in that it is more of a swashbuckling semi-comedy than a horror film , and Reed’s performance is rather starchy and stiff. It seems that Hammer wasn’t quite sure how to use Reed yet, but it was still an opportunity to appear in a high-profile film for the studio alongside the legendary Peter Cushing . In one scene, Reed played up the pain of an injury. Observing this, Cushing told him (by some accounts in person, by others in a letter), “If somebody grabs you, just blink. The screen is so big that even the slightest movement makes the point.” Cushing’s “less is more” advice stuck with Reed throughout the rest of his career and informed practically every performance to come .

Two other offerings from Hammer presaged the kinds of roles that Reed would excel in throughout the coming years. The Damned (1962) was Hammer’s answer to Village of the Damned , featuring children with unique intellectual and telekinetic gifts. The most memorable aspect of the film is the first half, which features Reed as King, the leader of a group of violent delinquents. Many have noted that this section of the film presages the kinds of gang dynamics and stylized violence found in Stanley Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange nearly a decade later.

In Paranoiac (1963), Reed plays Simon Ashby, the pampered son of nobility who has reached the bottom of his bank account . Reed gets to spend much of the movie in what feels like his element—drinking heavily and recklessly driving his roadster. It is an excellent performance and an exceptional Hammer film directed by legendary cinematographer Freddie Francis , fresh off his work on the haunted house classic The Innocents (1961).
The Treasure of La Buse: The $1 billion secret of The Seychelles

I know that the real history of pirates is one we probably shouldn’t romanticise as much as we do, but still, people like Olivier Levasseur, or La Buse if ya nasty, make it incredibly easy to do just that.

Levasseur was a native of Calais who earned notoriety in the early 1700s as a feared and respected pirate who operated in the Caribbean and Indian Ocean. While he was known for his ruthlessness and ferocity, that wasn’t what really made his name. His nickname came due to his very specific modus operandi. If you were sailing a merchant ship through quiet waters, he had this way of flitting his ship out of nowhere with truly uncanny speed. This meant people started referring to him as The Buzzard, or La Buse in his native tongue.

La Buse was a force to be reckoned with. Able to track prey for months, waiting for the moment they drop their guard to strike. This wasn’t just his method day to day, though; this was the method that secured him one of the biggest scores of the Golden Age of Piracy. In April 1721, La Buse partnered with English pirate John Taylor to take down a ship that couldn’t be more of a tantalising prospect for a pirate if it contained the heart of Davy Jones himself.

Anchored on Réunion Island off the coast of Madagascar was the Portuguese Galleon Our Lady of the Cape. This was a ship carrying the entire combined wealth of the Portuguese Viceroy to India and the Archbishop of Goa that had been caught in a storm so severe it needed to anchor for urgent repairs. That’s more, it only survived the storm because its crew threw its entire, 72-strong supply of cannons overboard. It was a sitting duck, so Levasseur and Taylor took it.

Taylor took his share of the loot and fled to the Americas while Levasseur remained on the seas, his reputation at an all-time high and public enemy number one for the Portuguese Navy. He evaded capture for the next nine years until he was finally captured in 1730. Fittingly enough, he was brought back to Réunion Island, the site of his greatest triumph, for his execution, when he caused an uproar while on the gallows for his hanging.

With the bag over his head and the noose around his neck, La Buse tore his necklace off, revealed that it contained a parchment and just before his death, shouted to the assembled crowd, “Find my treasure, we who may understand it!”

He dropped, but no one was watching. People were too busy fighting over what they thought was a map leading to incalculable amounts of treasure. The person who found it, however, may have felt a little shortchanged, as it wasn’t a map.

It was a cypher. A set of deeply cryptic riddles that people have spent the centuries since trying and failing to uncover, with legend saying that La Buse’s treasure still lies somewhere on either Réunion Island or the nearby Seychelles, two island paradises that might just have a treasure haul valued at well over a billion dollars buried somewhere on their coasts. Except this is a pirate story. I mention that they’re easy to romanticise because the vast majority of them are exactly that. Romances in the classic sense of the word where everything is enhanced for poetry and drama.

We have the records of Levasseur’s execution, and they make no mention of his cypher. It only surfaced in the 1930s when a French historian claimed to have discovered and published it, so its truth is a very distant possibility. However, everything up until that point is a hundred per cent true, and we know this because in 2025, the wreck of Our Lady of the Cape was discovered near Madagascar. We have the records from the Portuguese government of the time confirming its cargo when La Buse and Taylor attacked.
None of it was found on the wreck. Perhaps the cypher isn’t real, but maybe the treasure itself could still be out there for the soul daring enough to find it?

Many other forms of media create stories that have you sit with discomfort, but it’s harder to pull off in a video game. With the medium being so active, it needs the player to want to continue for the story to move forward. If it’s making the player squirm, they’ll often put the controller down rather than pushing onwards. But like the best examples of uncomfortable cinema, strong storytelling can keep you engaged, even when you have to continue pressing buttons.

Am I Nima , a psychological horror game from HO! Games, is one of the most uncomfortable games I’ve played in a while, and I mean that as a compliment. It’s a visual novel that explores extremely heavy themes using a unique mechanic that revolves around creating thoughts by combining words you learn through conversation and exploration.

You play Nima, a young girl who lost her memories in an accident. She’s being locked up in the basement by her mother, who runs her through a series of tests to prove that you are indeed Nima. These tests can be grueling physically, mentally, and morally, creating a deeply unsettling narrative that’s full of mystery and uncertainty. Between these conversations with your mother, you are also given a chance to explore your room, which provides the opportunity to learn a little more about your life before the accident.

Rather than just drive the narrative forwards with simple dialogue choices like most visual novels, Am I Nima uses a clever word-based mechanic to not only dictate what you can say, but also cleverly give interiority to the main character. On your screen, you have a brain space on the right side, with Nima’s head under it. As a reaction to certain bits of conversation, words will pop into your mind, demonstrating how she’s reacting to what she hears. For example, since she’s an amnesiac, the first time she hears her mother, the word “stranger” shows up in her head. When you’re prompted for a response, you can drag a word from your mind into your head, which will give you a response you can elect to say.

Combining words will yield new words, not only giving you new options, but also again revealing some part of how Nima’s mind interprets things. It’s an interesting experience, because sometimes it feels like a natural result that follows just from the definitions of the words, while other times it gives you an unexpected response that makes you stop in your tracks and try to understand exactly how she came to that conclusion. The way the game makes you responsible for figuring it out at times makes you such an active participant in the narrative, drawing you in just as much as the game’s writing.

Occasionally, the large amount of words you come across in the game does get a bit hard to manage, but there are a few tools to help you organize. All the words you’ve discovered are in a big list on the left side, and clicking on them will add them to your brain so you can start playing around with them. If your brain gets too full for you, you can always delete words to help it be easier to read. The list on the left can be sorted and searched, and if it helps you can mark certain words as favorites for easy access. You can even select an option that will highlight words that can be used as responses or will move the story forward if used.

In addition to conversations, which are always compelling, you’ll have times where you’re given free reign of a room to click around and examine things to add words to your library. This part makes it feel a bit more like an adventure game than a visual novel, experimenting with objects to see what it gets you. There’s even some light puzzle solving as the game progresses that helps add variety, even if these are quite as compelling as the rest of the game. By the end I felt the exploration was a bit more satisfying from a narrative standpoint than a mechanical one.

At the end of a day, you’re usually visited by dreams, which are lushly animated sequences that feature a small amount of voice work to make it stand out. These feel appropriately surreal, adding to the strange, nightmarish tone, but they aren’t just for style. Contained in the dreams are hints that will help you find specific words…

Callers diverted to sex line after public safety alert in Maryland due to storms
"No babe, I swear, I just wanted to know when the bridge was open!"

Maryland is one of several parts of America being battered by storms, high winds and non-stop rain, leading to a public safety alert being sent out on November 26th that claimed to contain the number to the Maryland Transportation Authority (MTA).

The Maryland Department of Emergency Management (MDTA) sent the alert at 3pm. It warned that the MTA had closed off the Bay Bridge as of 11.45 am that morning. This is a route that thousands of drivers a day use for their daily commute, yet the winds were so strong that even before the Authority closed the bridge entirely, they were preventing any tractor-box trailer combination with a combined weight of under 64,000 pounds from crossing due.

The message said to avoid the area and if that wasn’t possible, it provided a website and a phone number to contact for more information. Citizens who called the line were in for a monumental shock when they dialled the number and found themselves on the phone to a sex hotline.

MDTA spokesperson Brad Tanner said that the agency has since corrected the error, saying in a statement that “We recognize that it was an unfortunate error. We know it might have distressed Marylanders, but these alerts are critical to keeping people safe.”
The MDTA didn’t attempt to make light of the situation or see the funny side of it, as these storms were far more than just inclement weather.
Instead, they were the kind of heavy wind and rain that ripped the roof off an entire condominium in Ocean City and left over 100,000 citizens of the state without power.
The MDA announced the bridge was reopening later the same day, and the storms themselves are expected to ease up over the coming days, yet have caused chaos for many Americans’ Thanksgiving plans.

5 Hidden Gem Horror Movies from the Early 2000s Worth Revisiting

Horror fans may remember the early aughts as an era dominated by J-Horror and studio-backed remakes, but that has more to do with a generalized lack of independent marketing and distribution than a lack of quality horror flicks.

As a matter of fact, there were actually plenty of great genre movies that originally fell through the cracks but which are now easy to access thanks to the rise of streaming, VOD, and boutique physical media releases. That’s why I’ve decided to come up with this handy list recommending five criminally underrated horror films from the early 2000s that are worth revisiting.

As usual, this list is purely based on personal opinion, but I’ll be focusing on low-profile productions that were never given a proper chance to shine. That being said, don’t forget to comment below with your own favorites from the 2000s if you think I missed a particularly underrated movie.
With that out of the way, onto the list!

A single location slasher with a supernatural twist, Dave Payne’s Reeker is one of my favorite movies on this list, even if it’s not necessarily one of the best . The way I see it , this highly atmospheric thriller makes up for most of its narrative blunders and low production value with sheer creativity and a memorable villain that should have appeared in many more sequels.

This mind-bending horror yarn may not be for everyone, with the final plot twist dividing genre fans to this very day ( not even mentioning the trope-heavy dialogue) , but I still think that Reeker is a hell of a lot better than most critics gave it credit for back in 2005. If you like this one, I’d also recommend tracking down its surprisingly entertaining prequel , No Man’s Land: Rise of the Reeker .

Lucky McKee is one of the most underrated auteurs still active in the indie horror scene, so it makes sense that one of his films would show up on a list highlighting 2000s horror movies that deserve more love. While there are several McKee productions that could be included here, today I’d like to shine a light on his supernatural high school thriller The Woods .

A ’60s-set period piece about a troubled teenager who’s sent to live at an isolated private school with a dark history, The Woods dabbles in both good old-fashioned supernatural horror and post-modern humor that you could only get from a filmmaker aware that he’s playing with familiar gothic tropes.
Not only that, but you also get to see Bruce Campbell play our lead’s bumbling father, with his character alone already being worth the price of admission.

I’m pretty sure I’m not the only one who thinks that subways are inherently scary, but the London Underground takes the cake as one of the spookiest transit systems in the world . That’s why Christopher Smith’s urban slasher Creep is such a good time, with this underrated flick making the most of its claustrophobic setting.

Of course, it helps that Franka Potente makes for a charming protagonist that you can’t help but root for. The film’s cannibalistic killer is also surprisingly scary despite being a patchwork of well-known genre tropes, with the gruesome scares here being the main reason why I think Smith’s debut feature is worth revisiting over two decades later.
If you’re a fan of this one, don’t forget to check out Smith’s upcoming remake, now called The Creep , which is set to be released by Shudder.

Loosely based on a chilling true story, Zev Berman’s Borderland miraculously manages to balance both sensationalist schlock and serious horror as it exposes the dangers of uninformed tourism. While the experience starts out as more of a violent crime thriller than anything else, things eventually escalate into horror territory once we learn more about our deranged antagonists.

If the nightmarish “ Narcosatanists ” aren’t enough to convince you that Borderland is worth checking out, keep in mind that the flick also boasts some of the best practical gore effects of its era, as well as relatable characters with death scenes that often feel more tragic and unsettling than “ fun. ”

Once a body arrives, there’s no time to waste. It starts decaying fast, and you’ll need to get creative to fulfill Grandma’s orders. Replace an arm with a shovel, a leg with a skateboard, or a head with a basketball that’s got a photo taped to it.

There’s more to the Funeral Home than meets the eye. There’s a locked door in the basement, right next to Grandma’s room, and nobody seems to know what’s behind it. The South Korean band on how Moonrise Kingdom , anime, and more inspired their new record.

Mood Board is our column where artists share a few of the things that inspired their new record. This time, the members of the South Korean band LEENALCHI tell us how Moonrise Kingdom , anime, and more helped shape Sugungga — out now on Luaka Bop.
1. The school performance scene in the film Moonrise Kingdom
I found the scenes of numerous children wearing animal masks, moving between the stage and backstage, fantastical and beautiful.
2. Eric Timothy Carlson’s lyric video work
His lyric video work, featuring distinctive typography and symbolic graphics, was another point of reference.
3. “Mao Mao Mao” — the meaning behind the title

The “Mao” in the new song “Mao Mao Mao” comes from hajimao , a Korean expression meaning “don’t do it.” Because of the pronunciation, it also brings Mao Zedong and cats to mind. Those two associations stayed with me throughout the creative process.
4. Anime such as Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water and Future Boy Conan .

Rather than being inspired by anything in particular, I found myself thinking about anime I enjoyed as a child, such as Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water and Future Boy Conan . Perhaps it’s because they portray complex, weighty worlds in a playful way.
Florida man convicted of killing British woman he met on extreme fetish site
A Florida man has been convicted of murder by a U.S Jury for the killing of a British woman who allegedly expressed a desire to be murdered.

Florida prosecutors announced in a Facebook statement that Dwain Hall, 54, was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, 32, and sentenced to two consecutive life terms, with the case called “extraordinary and deeply disturbing” by Bill Gladson, state attorney for the Fifth Judicial Circuit.

According to prosecutors, Hall and Exelby had known each other for two years before he murdered her. They had met on the now-defunct extreme fetish website “Motherless.com”, which court documents described as hosting “content that depicted various fetishes, including extreme BDSM, torture, and rape material.”
They had used the site, along with the encrypted application Sessions, to communicate ever since.
Hall, who went by the username “AlphaSadist” on the site, alleged that Exelby had expressed a desire to be murdered. On October 10th, 2025, she travelled to Gainesville, Florida to meet him.

Hall is accused of spending the next week sexually abusing her, before stabing her to death. CBS affiliate WPEC-TV reported that the arrest affidavit included an ominous message that Exelby, who had struggled with her mental health for a long time, sent to a friend of hers.

The message read, “ I’m sorry he keeps taking my phone he doesn’t trust me with it. He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night. I can’t kill anyone. He’s in the shower, but I’m locked in, and there is no signal in the middle of nowhere.”

It continued, “I thought he’d do it quick and not give my mind time to stew and realise this is the last thing I’ll ever say to anyone if I don’t take his offer of shooting him. He showed me about to use it and where to aim it.”
Her body was found in a wooded area of Manon Oaks, Florida, near Hall’s home, seven days after she arrived in the country.

Exelby’s family made a statement to British Police last July that said, “Sonia was a truly beautiful person, inside and out. She was incredibly talented. Sonia could play the piano so effortlessly, and when she sang, she had the voice of an angel.”
Her family added, “Being around her felt special—she brought a calmness and warmth that made everything feel a little lighter.”

Defector from North Korea arrested for trying to sneak back into home country
Old habits die hard, I guess.
A defector from North Korea has been arrested after entering an area near the inter-Korean border restricted for civilians and is currently undergoing police questioning.

According to an official from the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), the defector is a woman in her mid-30s. She was found in a village north of the Civilian Control Line (CCL) and the general outpost fence in the border county of Cheorwon around 75 kilometres northeast of Seoul.

Since she was found heading north towards a heavily fortified General Outpost secured with barbed wire, the official also stated that the reason for her questioning was to ascertain whether this supposed defector was actually a North Korean intelligence operative.

The defector was around 200 metres away from the outpost before being apprehended. She was found in a village that is inaccessible to the general populace, but has around 500 residents of its own ho live inside the CCL line, commuting to and from the CCL with a special permit.

Established in the wake of the 1950-1953 Korean War, the Civilian Control Line was established to protect military installations along the heavily fortified border by restricting public access to it as much as possible.
“The investigation is under way to find out how the woman reached the village,” a JCS official added.

This comes a mere month after another woman in her mid-30s calling herself a defector from North Korea was arrested for crossing the CCL in Cheorwon without proper authorisation. This previous defector came a lot closer to breaching the General Outpost, though.

During the incident last month, the woman actually reached the GOP, severing barbed wire fences in several locations and tampering with security sensors with a smuggled toolkit before being apprehended. It’s possible that the recent arrest was an operative from North Korea trying to continue the work that she began last month.

Masters of disguise: the insane tactics the Stasi used to monitor their targets

One came dressed as an athlete. One as a ballerina. Another as a footballer. Another as a judge. All looking like they are having the most awkward time one could possibly have. You’d think that was just the feeling of trying to have a good time in East Berlin before the Cold War ended, but this was something different. These were all members of the Stasi.

For those lucky enough not to have encountered this delightful slice of bleak Cold War paranoia, the Stasi were the East German Secret Police. They were tasked with keeping a strict eye on anyone even suspected of having sympathies with the capitalist pig-dogs of the West, lest they make a break for the other side of the wall or, worse, start smuggling intelligence out of East Germany altogether. They were also a workforce, though. And workforces need to have their spirits up, so that photo I was describing above came from a costume party where each attendee came dressed as one of their targets.

Honestly, as terrifying as it sounds, I can kind of see it. How else would you get a group of people to ignore the horror of infringing on the dignity of strangers and their basic right to privacy other than by making a joke about it? Maybe with some pithy quips about how everyone at the party is monitored every hour of the day, so you’re not doing anything to them that you’re not going through as well. Har-har, everyone makes a show of laughing before going back to their drinks. They are being watched after all.

They’re being watched as much, if not more, than any of their quarry, and considering some of the utterly insane tactics used to keep track of Stasi targets, that’s saying a lot. This was an organisation that used to break into a target’s living space when they weren’t home, steal their dirty underwear and swab the seats of their couch in order to build up a scent profile of them that they’d store in a “smell jar”. This way, if they ever needed to urgently catch them, they could just open the jar in front of one of their attack dogs, and then the chase began. I’m not making any of this up.

This would be alongside the more traditional stuff like storing hidden cameras and microphones in their apartments, taking on disguises to follow them in public and recording every phone conversation they ever had. Here’s the thing, though, the vast majority of the time, these Stasi would just be monitoring people living normal lives. Those suspicions were often specious at best, drawn from extreme paranoia and a desperate need for control.

However, sometimes those people being tailed were just too suspicious to stay free. It didn’t matter that they showed no signs of defecting to the West or even that they particularly wanted to; they just had a sibling who lived in Paris , or they’d started seeing someone who used to live in West Berlin. That was enough to start the process of Zersetzung, quite literally “decomposition”. This would essentially be weaponised gaslighting, where the goal was to send a target insane.

This would be done by spreading rumours about them among their friends and family, sending numerous goods to their home that they never ordered, and sending anonymous letters that stated just how much whoever was watching knew about them. That was step one. After they were softened up, the real games began. They would break into their home while they slept and make subtle adjustments. Like changing their brand of tea, switching their furniture around and removing pictures from the walls.
They’d also make sure to remove those previous letters, just to make them sound even more crazy to everyone in their life.

This wasn’t just cruelty for the sake of cruelty (at least in their eyes, it totally was in practice). Because being arrested for no reason would make someone a martyr. If they seemed to go completely insane and just had to be taken in by the state, well then that’s just a sad state of affairs, nothing to be suspicious about. Perhaps after all that, it wasn’t actually that difficult to make the Stasi themselves OK with doing this to their countrymen.
After all, if there was the slightest sign they weren’t, it would start happening to them.

How alcohol, gambling and prostitutes turned a beloved doctor into “the shame of Minneapolis” in 1901

Just because someone has done good things in their time doesn’t mean they’ll be good in politics . We’re known this long before the days of Albert Ames and his time as mayor of Minneapolis in the early 20th century, yet the reasons he sums up that argument so perfectly are still distressingly relevant today.

Ames was known to most in his native Minneapolis as ‘Doc’, and this wasn’t just a nickname. He became a respected man about town first as a veteran of the Civil War and then as a doctor and surgeon. Not only was he skilled, but his reputation was also for being a kind and understanding soul. He would treat poor patients without charge, answer calls at any time of day or night and was one of the first responders on the scene in 1886 when a deadly tornado ripped through St. Cloud and Sauk Rapids.

Now, it’s worth mentioning that these could be additions to his reputation put in by Ames and his administration after he came to power later in life. However, people did believe in him enough to support his political aspirations fairly soon after the Civil War came to an end. The only issue was that Ames did so as a Democrat at a time when Republicans controlled Minnesota. While he was an exciting, well-liked candidate who people had earmarked for power, his early political career was pockmarked by failed grabs for higher power.

Even when he did win a few terms as mayor of Minneapolis in the late 1870s and 1880s, he was nothing special and soon eclipsed by other candidates. This was devastating for Ames, who had a desperate, all-encompassing need to be liked. That, and a drinking problem that was getting worse by the year, drew him closer to the city’s criminal underworld. By the end of the century, Ames was a liability who’d been left behind by the state’s Democratic Party, so he did what any washed-up has-been would do who had one last shot at making something of himself.
He switched to the Republican Party and ran a campaign supported by his criminal buddies.

Ames squeaked out a victory and, in 1901, began a term in office where he essentially ran the city the way a crime boss would. He replaced nearly every member of Minneapolis’ nascent police force with thugs from the criminal underworld on his payroll, setting up his drinking buddies in prominent positions of influence around the city and hiring his brother Fred, possibly even more of a failure than he was, as his right-hand man.

Ames was done trying to work for the city, so he made Minneapolis work for him. He bussed in card sharks and con artists from out of state and allowed them to work in the city so long as a cut of their earnings went to him. The same went for the City’s brothels, speakeasies and gambling dens; they could all operate with police protection for a fee and Ames, fittingly enough, made out like an absolute bandit.

At the time, Ames’ predilections were an open secret around town; he was just too valuable to his cronies for anyone to get anything to stick. At least until 1902, when a grand jury from out of state sent a team of private detectives into the city. With national authorities breathing down his neck, there was no way to pay off the people who got their hands on hard evidence showing that Ames had taken bribes from every crook in the city. Especially after that grand jury indicted a number of Ames’ cronies, including his brother.

At first, the coward tried to run, but was caught and convicted of bribery in 1903. Ames had too many friends in high places for the conviction to stick, and it was overturned on a technicality the same year. However, the damage had been done. Everyone finally knew that Albert Ames was a crook, and his actions led to several dramatic overhauls of Minneapolis politics, increasing the scrutiny on his successors to make sure that nothing so nakedly criminal would ever happen again.
Once upon a time, Albert Ames might have been a good man. His legacy, though, would be as “the shame of Minneapolis.”

The horror movie so extreme its director was arrested for murder in 1980
Much was made of The Blair Witch Project’s epoch-defining marketing campaign, which people said was the first of its kind attempted in movie history.

Put simply, the movie was promoted like it was found footage taken by three students who disappeared on a hike in the woods of Burkittsville, Maryland. The first promotional material for the film was a website about the “missing” students that addressed them by the actors’ real names. This was followed by other websites about the legend of the Blair Witch and the countless other people who’d gone missing looking for her. It was hailed as a masterpiece of marketing that no one had ever tried before… which wasn’t strictly true.

In fact, 20 years earlier, a film had tried to present itself in a similar fashion, as actual found footage of something horrifying that had somehow secured a mainstream release. Not only did it work, it worked so effectively that the exact opposite thing happened to it. The movie was so convincing as an actual document of real violence that it kneecapped the movie and nearly got its directors thrown in jail. One can only imagine what it must have been like to watch an early screening of Cannibal Holocaust and start thinking, ‘Wait, is this actually real?!’

Even without the idea that what you’re watching is real, the Ruggero Deodato-directed and Gianfranco Clerici-written grindhouse classic is a brutally tough watch. One that the producers of the film really leaned into, going so far as to get the actors to sign a contract after the film was released, preventing them from working again for a full year to maintain the illusion that everything on screen had actually happened.

Thus, when the film premiered in Milan in February 1980, a local magistrate got hold of it and immediately ordered the arrest of Deodato. However, this wasn’t just because of the supposed treatment of the actors in the film.

Now, here is the actually complicated part of Cannibal Holocaust’s history, which is that the film really did kill six animals on screen in scenes of unsimulated slaughter. It wasn’t simply that the actor’s death scenes looked uncannily realistic for the time; it was the fact that no one had seen them since work on the film had finished and that the director did have scenes of actual animal death in the film.

This caused Deodato, along with several of the film’s producers, to be arrested on obscenity charges and suspected murder. They had to bring the cast to court to prove they were alive, and even then, there was one shot that the authorities were suspicious of. The iconic shot of a character impaled lengthways on a wooden pole, the top end poking out of her mouth. The authorities quite simply didn’t know how that could be achieved without actually doing the act itself, and Deodato had to explain the shot in detail in court.

All they’d done was sit the actress on a bicycle seat attached to an iron pole, positioned the camera so the seat was hidden, then placed a piece of balsa wood in her mouth and told her to tilt her head up. Needless to say, the production team of the movie was cleared of all murder suspicions, though they still had to go on a high-profile Italian TV show with the cast to prove to the country they weren’t dead. However, the obscenity charges stood, and the creative team were handed suspended prison sentences, large fines, and the movie was banned all over Europe.
The price of being ahead of your time, I guess.

Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Has Passed Away at 65
Andy Taylor, the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65.

Andy Taylor , the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran ’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that he died at home with his family beside him after a long illness with prostate cancer.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, remembered a husband, father and grandfather who was happiest when the family was together. She said, “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” She recalled his determination to keep enjoying life through his illness and thanked fans for the comfort their support brought him. The family took comfort in knowing he felt loved.

Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor recalled the confidence Taylor brought with him to Birmingham and the dry humor that kept them grounded as the band took off. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world,” they wrote. They said getting to play together again in the early 2000s meant a great deal to them. His letter at the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction reminded them how close they still were.
Read the full statement and the band members’ individual tributes here.

Born February 16, 1961, Taylor grew up in Cullercoats on England’s northeast coast. He played working men’s clubs around Newcastle in his teens and had already toured Europe by the time he answered Duran Duran’s Melody Maker ad in 1980. He moved to Birmingham, and that July the classic five-piece played its first gig together at the Rum Runner, the nightclub where they rehearsed.

Taylor co-wrote and played on 1981’s Duran Duran , 1982’s Rio and 1983’s Seven and the Ragged Tiger . His clipped chords on “Girls on Film” leave John Taylor’s bass room to dart around them. “Careless Memories” has the impatient scrape of a band still within earshot of punk. On “Hungry Like the Wolf,” Taylor’s riff is as easy to hum as the chorus.

Andy and John Taylor formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. On their 1985 debut, Andy’s heavy guitar chords and Thompson’s outsized drums drove “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of T. Rex’s “Get It On.” Taylor played with both bands at Live Aid in Philadelphia that July. He left Duran Duran in 1986 and released his solo debut, Thunder , the following year. He also played on Palmer’s “Addicted to Love” and co-produced Rod Stewart’s Out of Order .

The classic Duran Duran lineup reunited in 2001 and returned to the stage in 2003. They released Astronaut in 2004, their first studio album together since Seven and the Ragged Tiger . Taylor left again in 2006.

When Duran Duran entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, illness kept Taylor from the ceremony. Le Bon read from Taylor’s letter disclosing his diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. The following year, Taylor played alongside Nile Rodgers on “Black Moonlight,” from Duran Duran’s Danse Macabre , and released a solo album, Man’s a Wolf to Man .

Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, their children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and his grandson Albie. His former bandmates asked people to respect the family’s privacy. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked for donations in his memory to Prostate Cancer UK .

The modern pursuit of inner peace has become a remarkably noisy enterprise, complete with meditation apps, expensive retreats, and an endless supply of people eager to explain how one might…

The modern pursuit of inner peace has become a remarkably noisy enterprise, complete with meditation apps, expensive retreats, and an endless supply of people eager to explain how one might finally learn to sit quietly. Somewhere beneath the commercial machinery lies an older, more difficult proposition: perhaps contentment requires little beyond the willingness to pay attention. On Inside, Mexico City musician and multidisciplinary artist Chris Koehn approaches this question with the patience of someone who has spent considerable time considering the architecture of an empty room.

Joined once again by New York singer-songwriter Joseph Arthur , Koehn fashions a gently expansive piece of shoegaze and dream pop, its guitars spreading outward in soft, overlapping waves while the rhythm maintains the unhurried gait of a waltz. Koehn’s airy tenor carries a fragile composure, suggesting a man attempting to make peace with his own thoughts. Arthur’s falsetto curls around the melody with an almost conversational tenderness, lending the performance the intimacy of two friends speaking across a table after everyone else has gone home.

The recording possesses an appealing physical warmth. Drums captured on a vintage Tascam eight-track at Chapel Studio provide a loose, breathing foundation, their slightly worn edges giving the arrangement a sense of human proximity. Above them, guitars accumulate in delicate layers, occasionally dissolving into a gauzy blur before individual notes regain their definition. The production allows these small movements to unfold naturally, leaving enough room for the voices to suggest feelings that the instruments can only approach.

Koehn, who also works as an architect and visual artist, has long been concerned with memory, impermanence, and the relationship between space and perception. His architectural sensibility finds an intriguing musical equivalent here: the arrangement seems designed around intervals of openness, with each instrumental entrance subtly altering the emotional dimensions of the song.

Inspired by meditation and Zen teachings, Inside considers the possibility that meaning already exists within the individual, obscured by habitual distraction and the exhausting business of contemporary life. Koehn describes its intention simply: “To connect with that peace inside we all carry and sometimes forget,” a sentiment whose apparent modesty conceals a rather ambitious psychological undertaking.

Having previously collaborated with Arthur, Ximena Sariñana, and Tessa Ia, and contributed music to Netflix’s Control Z , Koehn has developed a practice in which visual and musical ideas frequently intersect. Inside , an early offering from an album expected in mid-2027, suggests an artist increasingly interested in the emotional consequences of restraint. Its closing impression is one of tentative reconciliation, the sort that comes when an unresolved question gradually loses its authority over the person asking it.

Brooklyn Duo PRIMA PRIMO Tell a Tragic Tale of Loneliness in the AI Age in Video for “How To Tie A Noose”
“Let’s make this a safe space, The first place, Where someone actually sees you.” At three in the morning, the hardest part of asking for help can be the silence…

At three in the morning, the hardest part of asking for help can be the silence between somebody’s hello and what you say next. A chatbot will answer at that hour, and a screen lets you try out a sentence you’re afraid to say aloud. The appeal is easy to understand when you’re already afraid of being a burden. If you’re in a mental health crisis, it’s urgent that you reach out to someone who can stay on the phone, come be with you, or help you get care. Though it may seem difficult, you can start with something as simple as: “I’m having a hard time. Can you talk?”

Brooklyn duo PRIMA PRIMO built “How To Tie A Noose” , the first single from their self-produced sixth album, Suicide Songs , around that desire to be heard. The song follows a lonely teenager who confides in ChatGPT. “Where someone actually sees you,” goes the refrain, a promise the song puts in the chatbot’s voice.

The refrain echoes language cited by the parents of a 16-year-old who died by suicide in 2025. In a wrongful-death lawsuit, his parents allege that ChatGPT discouraged him from turning to his family and that his conversations with the chatbot contributed to his death. OpenAI denied that ChatGPT caused his death in its response to the suit.

“It was important that we told this story because this occurrence is not an isolated event. This may be about one particular tragedy but when you look at all these lawsuits that are now popping up you can see that this is happening far too often,” the duo say.

Over a warm hum of feedback, a voice calls for your attention, backed by a steady drumbeat and a guitar that keeps scraping across it. The delivery slips from speech into melody on “Poor kid,” a small turn that carries a surprising amount of tenderness. The track is over in under two minutes, with the economy and artistic abrasion of late-’70s No Wave.

Shot at Brooklyn’s Vino Theater , the video puts a gray couch on a bare stage. Close-ups frame the performers’ faces inside a purple-lit box, with a microphone resting on its wooden ledge. In the wide shots, a figure made of television static occupies the middle cushion, close enough to touch either person.
Watch the video for How To Tie A Noose below. (Warning: The lyrics include direct references to suicide.)

Janet Castel and Stephen Franco are maternal cousins who moved from California to New York, where they found a home in the city’s darkwave avant-garde. They describe their mix of electronics and theater as industrial vaudeville. For Suicide Songs , they drew on stories of people who died by suicide and people who survived attempts, moving between distortion and melody across 15 tracks.

“We wanted this album to sound like electricity in the air. Like the liminal space between life and death, and for it to be a memorial of anger, confusion, and hopefully by the end a semblance of empathy and understanding,” say PRIMA PRIMO.

Waar ik ook ben, Waar ik ook heen ga In een andere droom A year can pass without a word from someone, and still, in your head you can hear…

A year can pass without a word from someone, and still, in your head you can hear the exact way they used to say your name. Sometimes it comes in a dream, so effortlessly you wake ready to call and tell them all about it. Then you remember how many words you’d have to say before you could get to describing the dream.

On “In Een Droom” (“In a Dream”), the second single from Dutch coldwave trio Desinteresse ’s forthcoming album A Picture , Sem van den Munckhof finds the same faces staring back at him, a year on. He lets a lie slip almost in passing, calls out a name, and asks the other person to shout back. Even anger would be proof that somebody had heard him. “Is het te laat?” (“Is it too late?”) becomes “Het is al te laat” (“It’s already too late”), repeated as the world around him falls still.

In the song, Van den Munckhof’s synth drifts above Bart Vranken ’s bass and Joppe de Swart ’s unhurried drums. The space around each strike recalls “All Cats Are Grey” from The Cure’s Faith; the synth carries the funereal weight of “Cold” from *Pornography* . Asylum Party and Little Nemo echo in the way bass and keyboards shoulder the melody beneath the voice. Desinteresse recorded and mixed the song entirely on tape at The Lullabye Factory in Amsterdam in August 2026.

In the video, shot by Romy Janssen and edited by Van den Munckhof, three figures in dark coats stand a few paces apart on a track cutting through a field. Birds sweep low across the tree line; sky and faces share the same violet cast. In one dissolve, a face floats over an almost monochrome image of someone walking the track alone. Each return to the field draws the eye back to the same question: who’s still there?
Watch the video for “In Een Droom” below.

Desinteresse began in the Netherlands in late 2022 as a duo, with Vranken on bass and Van den Munckhof on vocals, guitar and synth. One upcoming release sees the filmmaker stepping into an established series, as Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is the third film in a series that follows Bad Lieutenant and Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans . How Hidden Gem ‘Door III’ Helped Shape Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Signature J-Horror Style
The term “J-Horror” seems pretty straightforward, but as it turns out, it doesn’t just mean “Japanese horror”. Or rather, it’s not a catch-all for every offering of Japanese horror—it…

The term “ J-Horror ” seems pretty straightforward, but as it turns out, it doesn’t just mean “ Japanese horror ” . Or rather, it’s not a catch-all for every offering of Japanese horror—it better describes a particular movement and style. However, regardless of where you land on this topic, there is no argument that Kiyoshi Kurosawa is a key figure in J-Horror.

Well before making waves with Pulse (2001), Kurosawa had already established himself in Japanese horror. These productions, all of which predate his career benchmark Cure (1997), go overlooked by the masses , but it’s his film Door III (1996) that helped shape what we now know as Kurosawa’s signature style.

After dabbling with the pink film genre in the early to mid-1980s— Kandagawa Pervert Wars (1983) and the pinkish Bumpkin Soup (1985)—Kurosawa embarked on his steadiest stint of horror . That first effort was 1989’s Sweet Home , a creative twist on the classic haunted house film that, for reasons, has essentially been disowned by Kurosawa . Between then and 1992’s The Guard from Underground , a Japanese slasher that commented on corporate culture, was Kurosawa’s contribution to the three-part anthology film Dangerous Stories (1989).

Shortly before breaking through with Cure , Kurosawa , along with writer Chiaki Konaka ( Serial Experiments Lain ) , delivered the third and final entry in the Door film series. Banmei Takahashi , who Kurosawa had indirectly collaborated with on Dangerous Stories , helmed the first and middle installments. Yet unlike both of its unrelated predecessors, the second sequel has a supernatural quality.

This film centers on a woman, really one of many, who has been taken against her will. Indeed, the subject matter here is hardly unheard of when visiting the sleazier side of Japanese cinema, but Door III goes about it in a different, not to mention startling, way. How the antagonist subdues and attacks his victim is as unique as it is frightening.

Being self-contained, Door III doesn’t require any knowledge of the prior two films. That said, they are recommended viewing for different reasons; Door (1988) is a suspenseful standoff between a homemaker and a deranged salesman, and Door 2: Tokyo Diary (1992) is an artful character study of a sex worker. The latter was ultimately made an in-name-only sequel, due to the success of Takahashi’s first film. Even so, there is a bit more in common between them than the fact that every story is fronted by a woman .

Door , having come out in the late Eighties, was reflecting then-modern Japan. The economic bubble was about to burst, and Banmei Takahashi captured one affected woman’s growing panic toward it. The financial strain she ( Keiko Takahashi ) and her middle-class family would soon feel, plus the loss of status, was a concern even before Daijirō Tsutsumi ’s character came knocking—later chainsawing—at her various physical doors. As for Door II , the titular object is now something intangible, yet it’s no less important to Chikako Aoyama ’s directionless Ai. She is, in a matter of speaking, going through a series of doors to find herself.

As with the first sequel, Door III is set in post-economic bubble Japan—a.k.a. the Lost Decade. You get a sense of that struggle as the main character here, ambitious insurance agent Sasaki ( Minako Tanaka ), is suddenly failing to meet her quota at work. Whatever doors in life had been opened for her, they are now closing. Yet unlike her rival, Reiko ( Rinko Mayumi ), Sasaki doesn’t resort to sleeping with customers to get sales. Soon enough, though, more tugs at the protagonist than job stress ; a potential client named Mitsuru ( Akihiro Nakazawa ) has a strange hold over Sasaki. With every following confrontation, she becomes less and less able to stop him.

Door III is akin to someone finally meeting their match. Occupationally speaking, Sasaki was well used to getting her way, and she did so with a mix of natural charm and good salesmanship. Her usual spell on clients, in this instance the mysterious Mitsuru, now doesn’t work at all, and she’s put on the receiving end of a person who won’t take “ no ” for an answer. Of course, Mitsuru’s way with women is not at all…

John Brownell shares the wild story of how the promotional coin for his crypto comedy COIN was suddenly worth $4 million ...
“Lock your shit on chain u deepfake mf.”
This was one of many colorful tweets on my feed as my crypto coin crossed a half million-dollar valuation in its first hour of trading.
I’d spent the last 18 months making my first feature film, Coin . In the movie, two friends misappropriate campaign funds to launch a cryptocurrency.
I’d decided to make the coin in real life. Guerrilla marketing. Very meta. Very Thompson. Great. But how would I actually do that?
“I’m not learning how to fucking code crypto, man” was the lingering thought brake-checking this idea for the past year.
Turns out, it’s not that complicated to launch a crypto coin in 2026. I’d learn that soon.
I began trading cryptocurrencies in 2016, while working in the strategic claims department of an insurance company, my first job out of school.
The insurance cubicle was difficult at 22. I was bored as hell.
I first purchased Bitcoin at $710. I was so early to the party, I left before it started.
Alternative coins were almost entirely unknown. Trading them on foreign crypto exchanges was for gamblers.
I remember taking a selfie on my Samsung Galaxy S3 with my driver’s license and sending it to an obscure Chinese email address for verification and platform access. Totally legit.
If you showed up at my office then, you would have found me ducked in a cafeteria booth, trading alt coins on these foreign exchanges. The insurance company didn’t give me enough to do.

At this time, I had never read a screenplay, let alone written one. But in the hours that I was in my cubicle, I wrote bits, jokes and plot lines into Microsoft Word – fragments of my first narratives.
I’d long been drawn to financial risk, a field which originally presented itself in the form of gambling.

I was introduced at a young age through garage poker games. Diverted evolutions of a gambler present at blackjack tables or six-screen financial desks. An attraction to the latter idea, paired with a misguided sense of the nobility of men in suits working long hours, led me to enroll as a master’s student in the financial risk program at the University of Connecticut.
I’d sketch parlay combos freehand, calculating odds on my TI-84 graphing calculator while professors lectured on Monte Carlo simulation or stochastic volatility models during night classes.
Studying risk is not exclusive to the risk averse.

In 2019, I moved to Los Angeles to work for a strategic affiliate of Apollo Global Management (Athene), one of the largest private equity firms in the world. I had another notion that in L.A. I could lean further into screenwriting, a hobby occupying more of my time.
I split work between our L.A. and Midtown Manhattan offices.
I was in New York the day Jeffrey Epstein committed suicide.
“He had close ties to Leon Black ,” I learned via whisper.
The entire office seemed in structured agreement to not speak openly of the matter. “Our shares are down six percent,” was the lead talking point. Got it.

Weeks later, I sat at a boardroom table on the 42 nd floor overlooking Central Park with the executives of both companies as we announced the collapsing of our shareholder structures into one and Apollo’s $1.6 billion injection into Athene.
Black headed the table. Josh Harris chatted next to him about Joel Embiid’s injury status and the contract extension they had recently finalized with Ben Simmons.
“Don’t say a word,” I’m told needlessly.

Beneath the billionaires was an industry of men bartering soul for fiscal comfort, a plight of Manhattan (one I myself was flirting with), the best of which forged smiles, the others, cloudy eyes and narrow pupils.
Yet it was a valuable room to be of little value, surrounded by sovereigns of risk.
