talker and Alex Lahey Want to Make Art for Art’s Sake
The singer-songwriters catch up about creative rituals, surviving as a working artist, and more.

talker is the project of LA-based singer-songwriter Celeste Tauchar; Alex Lahey is a singer-songwriter based in Melbourne. The new talker record, Runaway Jane , just came out this summer, and to celebrate the release, the two friends caught up about creative rituals, surviving as a working artist, and more.
Celeste : I’m happy that we are doing this. I feel like it’s very classic us fashion — I leave for tour tomorrow and you leave for Australia on Saturday.
Alex : I know, right? So brutal.
Alex : Are you your most creative when you go away? Or are you your most creative when you’ve been away and you return?

Celeste : I think that I am most inspired when I’m away, but I don’t think that I do the act of creating as much until I’m back. I think that I’m gathering a lot. But I haven’t really gone anywhere this year — well, I did go to Australia. [ Laughs .]
Alex : It’s almost like January doesn’t count at this point. It feels so long ago.

Celeste : So long ago. Since then, I didn’t do summer travels much, other than little short wedding visits and stuff like that. And it’s interesting because I do think that I leaned really hard into creativity this year and into figuring out what that means for me, because I realized that I just want to be making stuff and living a creative, artful life. A lot of that does involve music; a lot of that involves making records and touring. But that can also mean a whole host of other things and not putting the pressure on always being in music work mode. So it’s interesting because I have felt very creative here, and I’m trying to maintain the practice of not running away to try to find that inspiration.
Celeste : Self-sufficiency, a thousand percent. Which is a very difficult skill. I mean, hilariously, my album that just came out, Runaway Jane , is kind of about that exact thing.
Alex : Wow, I didn’t even put that together. A beautiful segue. [ Laughs .]

Celeste : [ Laughs .] But it’s this thing of, do you rely on outside stimuli and other experiences that fill out of your life in order to allow yourself to be creative? Or do you make that a practice that’s just in your life no matter what you’re doing?

Alex : Yeah. It’s about enabling yourself in a way. I feel like it is a delicate balance of ritual and routine, and factoring in creativity into that. But then also kind of gaslighting yourself into being like, Oh, yeah, now’s the time . It’s always the time, but now’s the time. You know?

Celeste : I started doing affirmations and gratitude lists earlier this summer — thank you, Julia Cameron — which I still pretty much do every morning. The list has gotten so long because I keep adding stuff. So it’s like, “I am great at forming habits. I am a successful artist. I have a right to be an artist. My creativity is appreciated. People like me…” It’s two full pages because if I add something on, I don’t want to take something else away.

Alex : It’s interesting to have a log of an affirmation or a desire. These things are all a mirror. Isn’t that the whole thing with The Artist’s Way ? It’s kind of like you’re holding up a mirror to yourself as an artist, and there is a radical acceptance part of it?

Celeste : Oh, absolutely. I think there’s a lot about it that’s hokey. I’ve talked to people who are like, “I really couldn’t get through some of the exercises,” which, fair enough. But it’s holding up a mirror — it’s getting what you put into it. And I love a cheesy spiritual, artistic exercise anyway.

I think that there are things — I mean, yes, I put an album out this year. I’m about to go on tour. There are these little touchstones that on paper you’re like, “Yes, great, awesome.” But internally, I do feel like I didn’t do that much creatively this year. There was a lot of releasing and promoting and putting stuff out, but in terms of the actual creative process, I didn’t feel as connected to it. But what I really did get out of digging into a journaling practice: I think that I feel really happy with my life.
Celeste : I know. I’m embarrassed to say it.
Alex : No, you shouldn’t be. I mean, damn. That’s so deeply existential.

What should a festival line-up look like in 2026?
It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Emma Wilkes investigates the changing tides of festival line-ups, from the mainstream to the obscure.

The nights are long, the year is ending, and the once-yellowing grass is now carpeted with frost, but next summer is already taking shape. Every day, it seems, there’s another fresh festival line-up threatening to knock some digits off your bank balance. I should know – I spend this time of year writing news stories about them.

If you’re a regular festival goer, or even if there’s just one particular event you count down the days to return to, it’s a time of year that can bring bated breath and crossed fingers. It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Just like music itself, it’s subjective, and there can be a difference between a festival line-up that’s not to your taste and a line-up that’s an all-round failed throw.

In the last week, I’ve seen the internet split down the middle over two line-ups in particular. This year’s Manchester edition of Outbreak Festival was the most diverse yet controversial in its 15-year history, featuring “The Hayley Williams Show” headlining for two nights on the bounce and a line-up co-curated by Hayley Williams itself, with fewer traditional hardcore acts and wider-spanning alternative names including Wednesday, American Football and Julien Baker. Some were instantly hooked, others – especially Outbreak’s more traditional fans – feeling like the festival had changed beyond recognition.

A couple of days later, Glastonbury unveiled its line-up poster some months earlier than expected. It had the youngest headliners this side of the millennium, in the form of 33-year-old Sam Fender and Harry Styles and 25-year-old returning headliner Billie Eilish, while the rest of the bill leaned younger and more pop-heavy. The Instagram comments paint a divided picture, especially among older Glasto-goers feeling pushed out, or guitar fans feeling it was all a little anaemic with a limited offering for their tastes.

Neither of these are ‘bad’ bills, per se. The Outbreak line-up I love, and the Glasto line-up I appreciate but am relatively unmoved by. But viewed through a lens of objectivity rather than subjectivity, what makes a ‘good’ festival bill?

The crucial question is what a festival is for. Sure, it’s a weekend to dance with your friends, explore music, tick off bucket list bands and fill your head with memories, but every festival poster is a statement. What matters in music right now? Who do people want to see? It should hold up a mirror to what culture looks like, which obviously has commercial purposes as a means to promote an album, but there’s an element of artistic value to it too.

The relevant question to ask could be ‘Is it current?’, but not all festivals necessarily operate with that energy, so perhaps the better one is, ‘Is it relevant?’ Are you booking bands that feel of the moment, whether they’re breaking out or surging back into fashion, or milking the nostalgia cash cow?

Equally important is variety. What’s the use of booking the same bands that do the rounds every year, or the same sort of sounds? There’s an element of curation involved. What sort of vibe is the day going to have? How much choice is there of who to see at a particular time? And it goes without saying - if it’s mostly male and pale from top to bottom, it loses relevancy points. There’s something deeply retrograde about not taking heed of the genuinely meaningful calls for more people to see artists who look like them on festival stages.

There’s also an aspect of cultural responsibility too. The smaller stages of a festival can offer formative experiences for the heroes of the future to draw new fans in and develop how they perform. Festivals need to make the space to nurture that talent, especially those coming up through the grassroots. It’s why it felt like such a disappointment to see Reading and Leeds cut the BBC Introducing stage, and pad out its replacement stage, The Canopy, with nepo babies who may not need the boost. By contrast, the Cheltenham-based 2000trees has always been brilliant at building up new bands, booking them year after year, and creating a culture of what’s known as ‘Trees bands’ who the fans love just as much as they love the festival.
Punk's poet laureate settles into the NPR Music office with her band for a moving, close-knit set of spoken word and songs.

In some ways, Patti Smith 's performance at the Tiny Desk is a return to her roots. A universally revered and widely influential legend who's played some of the biggest stages in the world, Smith got her start as a poet and performance artist in more intimate spaces. After spending much of the past year touring to celebrate the 50th anniversary of her landmark debut album Horses , Smith and her band settled in at the NPR Music office on a sunny, late-summer afternoon for this moving, close-knit set of spoken word and songs.

Smith opens with a largely improvised tale about an aging sea captain who longs for one final and magical journey, before segueing into the winding and reflective "Nine," from 2012's Banga album. She follows with a yearning take on "Fireflies" from 1996's Gone Again , and the hopeful "Peaceable Kingdom" from 2004's Trampin' , which she dedicates to "all of the children globally who suffer the consequences of war." Smith closes with a soul-stirring version of "People Have the Power," a propulsive anthem to resistance and unity she wrote with her late husband and MC5 guitarist Fred "Sonic" Smith for 1988's Dream of Life .

They were cast out by the Christian music industry. Now they're speaking out
They were silenced or cast out for their perceived sins against evangelical Christianity. But a new film tells their whole story.
Nikki Leonti signed her first record deal at age 13, and soon found it came with expectations that she be a perfect model of evangelical morality.

In the early 2000s, Michael Passons was at the top of the Contemporary Christian Music world. His vocal pop group Avalon had earned trophies from the Christian music scene, but also found breakout mainstream success – an American Music Award, for example, in 2003.
"We were sitting right up there with Britney and Justin," Passon recalled.

During his late-'90s-to-early-2000s tenure, Avalon earned more than a dozen Christian number ones. But as the other group members married and he remained single, the suspicion that he was gay endangered that success.
"The Christian music business is a business," Passons said. "And in that culture, being a gay person was bad for business. So, everyone was gonna lose money."
In 2003, not long after the high of the American Music Awards, came a steep fall.

Passons says his bandmates ambushed him with the news that he had been kicked out of the group. They told a magazine he'd chosen to leave and quickly replaced him, while making Passons sign a nondisclosure agreement.

The entertainment industry has had its high-profile reckonings with abuse, first #MeToo, then the discourse around the R. Kelly and Diddy trials and collective reexamination of the tabloid scrutiny teen pop stars like Britney Spears faced.
Now, the new documentary Safe For the Whole Family finally applies that type of critical lens to the peak era of Christian pop: the 1990s.
Michael Passons, a former singer in the Christian band Avalon, is featured in a new documentary about the ways in which some musicians were silenced.

In the new documentary, which premiered at the Nashville Film Festival in September, Passons fully spells out what happened behind the scenes: his band mates, management and record label suspected he was gay and conspired against him to protect their bottom line.

"I was very aware of the deafening hypocrisy of the whole thing," he said, "that there's so many gay and queer people who have sung and composed amazing religious music. These people have contributed so much to Christian music, but yet the person is outcast."

Two of the Avalon members involved didn't respond to NPR's request for comment. The third, Melissa Greene, corroborated Passons' account in an email: "What Michael describes is what happened. I was in the room, and I take ownership of my part in it. We were inside a system that taught us his attraction was a danger to the ministry. I didn't think I was only believing a system. I thought I was believing God."
Greene said that years later, she realized she was wrong and asked Passons for forgiveness. "I'm grateful I finally owned how wrong I was, and grateful for his willingness to lean back in."

Passons was devastated by what amounted to a blacklisting; he couldn't even find work as a church music minister. But by the time he was approached about appearing in Safe For the Whole Family , he was ready to take part in the first-ever collective reckoning with how Christian pop treated some of its stars.
"We were all coming together as a voice for what it felt like to have our voices silenced," he said.

Jason Ikeler, the filmmaker behind the doc, grew up listening to these singers. He's also gay, and found himself alienated from evangelical Christianity and ready to make sense of the subculture he'd experienced.
In 2023, he began contacting his old Christian pop heroes, approaching them with care. "With a lot of them, it did feel like you're talking to a friend – you're like trauma-bonded," he said.

Ikeler reassured the performers whose perspectives he sought that this wouldn't be a scandalous takedown of Christianity: "I don't wanna make a super scathing thing. I want to tell the truth. I don't wanna sweep anything under the rug."

But revealing what transpired out of public view carries sizable risks for musicians whose work still intersects with Christian music even occasionally, like Nikki Leonti, who's written songs for a new generation of Christian artists.
"If you want to maintain good standing in Christian spaces, you can't do a documentary like this," Leonti said.

In 'GTA VI,' every stolen car is a music discovery machine
Amid the mega-success of 'Grand Theft Auto VI,' one feature has enthralled players: Each time you enter a vehicle, the in-game radio opens a musical rabbit hole to get lost in.
Protagonists Jason and Lucia lead the highly anticipated video game sequel Grand Theft Auto VI , which centers its pop soundtrack as players drive between missions and explore the open world.
Editor's note: This article contains spoilers for the early play hours of Grand Theft Auto IV .

If you've ever wondered what it might feel like to lead cops on a high-speed chase through downtown Miami as Young Thug croons, "Hustlers don't stop, they keep going," Grand Theft Auto VI has you covered. The massive open-world action game, which turns a one-to-one recreation of Florida's central hotspot — dubbed Vice City, Leonida — into the playpen for a Bonnie and Clyde-style outlaw campaign, is largely powered by music. There are currently more than 800 songs in the game, all of which have been spun off into bespoke radio stations representing the vibrant music culture of the place it simulates. Early into my playthrough, Kevin Lyttle's 2003 soca hit " Turn Me On " blared out of a speedboat's onboard radio as I pulled up to a yacht party, creating a unique thrill as the familiar suddenly became new again.

The most anticipated video game sequel of all time, and now among the most successful entertainment properties ever, GTA VI follows military vet Jason Duval and new parolee Lucia Caminos as they repair their broken relationship, cutting their teeth in a high-stakes criminal megalopolis with hopes of regaining custody of their son. Players split time between the two characters, playing linear missions that advance the story, triggering side quests that spiral into all corners of a vast map, or testing the limits of the open world by doing, well, whatever they want. Where similar games allow the user to "fast travel," or teleport, to important areas, GTA values the scenic route, the atmosphere that linear travel creates. And since hijacking rides is a core mechanic, that atmosphere is always changing: Each time you pull the door shut on a new exotic whip, helicopter or airboat, that vehicle's radio kicks on one of more than 20 stations spanning pop, rock, hip-hop, jazz, dance and classical. As reggaeton artist Rauw Alejandro noted of his playing experience in an interview with Billboard , "Sometimes, I wasn't even doing the missions — I was just vibing, discovering new things, listening to the music on the radio."
The Emotional Legacy Of 'Tony Hawk's Pro Skater'

The need to spend lots of time driving around in cars makes the user a captive audience, and as such, the radio is a pipeline — to old songs, newer songs, new-to-you songs and even a few new-to-everyone songs. A previously unreleased D'Angelo track can be found on the Gilles Peterson-hosted station Worldwide FM. When Jason picks Lucia up from prison, " Crazy for You ," a new song by Lana Del Rey, plays as they start their desperado journey together. Premieres from Burna Boy, Kali Uchis & Helado Negro, Zara Larsson and Cardi B are scattered across the stations. Beyond the exclusives, one of which pairs SZA with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, are relatively recent songs given new life by the narrative. Two versions of Carly Rae Jepsen's cult classic " Run Away with Me " soundtrack key scenes in the early game, a jet ski excursion turned supercar race to the nightclub NINE1NINE — and when Jason and Lucia get there, Tove Lo and SG Lewis' dance sleeper " Heat " is blaring. Deeper in are songs that will be familiar to many but are transformed by context. The couple's first string of robberies together has a sync so perfect I dare not spoil it.

The gameplay of GTA VI opens the door to a unique kind of sonic immersion, one that straddles classic radio functionality and the unique surreality that only video game storytelling allows. On one hand, the radio experience exposes players to a distinctly old-world curation on a scale that maybe isn't possible anywhere else, given the size of the player base. On the other, it treats most in-game playback like needle drops in a movie: highly subjective, there to make the player feel as much as possible like the star.

“This ridiculous rock ‘n’ roll myth”: Decade-spanning conversations with Manic Street Preachers
Manic Street Preachers have just announced their one-off Cardiff gig to celebrate 35 years of 'Generation Terrorists'.
What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Whereas The Fall, those bands in Seattle that just lived on hard drugs and strong coffee, Sex Pistols… they lived on bad motorway service station diets and they made the greatest music. I think if you care that much about your bodily health, you’re shutting off a pathway to creativity.
“But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit.”

If the small venues fed us, it was a bonus to be honest, but from what I remember, there were a lot of really lovely people who did. Even if there was some booze and crisps on the rider we were happy, really. But even if there was no food on offer we could usually find a local chippy, even though those are hard to find these days. Today, you can always find a Costa but not a chippy. James ranks the chip shops we visit and I think the ones we went to in Hull and Bridlington got full marks. In fact it was at the really big Army & Navy Stores in Hull that we kitted ourselves out with the clothes we’d wear during The Holy Bible period.

We’re back out on tour with Suede and we have to up our game because they’re so good live. Both bands were more than happy to contribute to the voluntary grassroots levy on this tour. You know, I’m still a real fan of music. I don’t want to deny bands the chance to tour that we had. The only other route for them is spending literally all of their time on social…

Last night marked the end of my birthday week, because spending last week in Paris wasn’t enough- I had to extend it. What a gig to wrap it up with! I’ve been waiting to see C.O.F.F.I.N for what has felt like a lifetime, and last night- I finally got to see them. What made it even more special was having Gold Cup as the support.

And to be honest, it won’t be long until they are headlining the Pink Room at YES. Some bands are made to be heard live, and Gold Cup are one of those bands. There’s something about their live shows that just makes you feel good and glad to be alive, y’know? I can’t wait for their debut record to come out because it’s just going to make their shows even more wild. They’re the best at what they do, and it felt like the crowd were an even split of Gold Cup and C.O.F.F.I.N fans, and you cannot help but be proud of that. The energy they have on stage and the way they play together is a thing of beauty- and yes, you will leave feeling like you want to start a band because of them.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. Part of me was watching the band, the other part was just obsessed with the crowd. It is so easy to feel unsafe at shows especially when it’s rowdy, but this felt safe. It felt like a community. And as a visibly queer person, that feeling is rare to find right now given how shit the world is. But when you find that safety net, you hold onto it. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. Life is tough enough already- just be kind to each other. It’s not hard.

Every song is yelled back at the band, and there are countless stage dives and crowd surfs. You could feel the love for the band in the room, truly. And the sense of being free and being able to express yourself however you want is also felt, and that’s something we should never take for granted. You can tell that the band not only love the bones of each other but they absolutely love playing shows, and you could feel how much it meant to them. I spent the time in awe of Ben because anyone who can sing AND drum at the same time is someone to admire (within reason because there are some people who can do it but y’know…)

Every song is greeted with people in the front throwing their sweaty bodies into each other and having the time of their lives. Some of them may be feeling it today but who cares! The joy on their faces, arms around their mates and strangers- it was so lovely to see because the world is unkind, but that energy did not step foot into the room once last night. What C.O.F.F.I.N have created with their music and live shows is a safe space, and that’s something to really hold onto. For me songs like Fast Love (this was my favourite and it was a tough call) and Give Me A Bite were WILD! Think Bad absolutely ripped too as did White Dog.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

Enter Shikari speak exclusively to DiS
3 things we learned from Rou Reynolds' return to the DiS podcast. Emma Wilkes summarises Sean's exclusive chat.

News of their hiatus took me by surprise. I thought of Enter Shikari as a band who could be life's constant - death, taxes, Shikari shows - one who I never imagined could have been anything but near-omnipresent titans of British live music. Maybe I didn't see the warning signs in the message from the Instagram video vocalist Rou Reynolds shared, in which he detailed how difficult 2026 had been for him, especially in relation to his mental health.

Explaining why Shikari had not played any shows since the surprise release of new album Lose Yourself in April, he said he had “been going through a lot of adversity that has brought my capacity to zero” , which involved burnout, OCD and nervous system sensitisation. He mentioned Shikari had been in discussions about their future as a band but had also written new music. I thought this would be one fraught chapter in a story with more to come.

But, of course, no-one is invincible. Sadly, but truthfully, no band can last forever. At the very least, they're going out in a manner that might be necessary, but it's still on their own terms, with a sense of dignity.

I'm seeing them live at Alexandra Palace in November, and I've got no idea how it's going to feel, or even if it's the last time I'll ever see them play. What I do know is the sadness will be felt incredibly widely, among a loyal fanbase for whom Shikari still feel like people's heroes, who have always stood on business, displaying solidarity years before it was even a buzzword.

Sean spoke to Rou on this week's Drowned In Sound podcast, a 90-minute deep dive into where his head has been in the last twelve months, and what his future might look like without Enter Shikari in it. Along the way, they take on everything from activism to mental health via nervous system regulation and, of course, being champions of the grassroots levy.
Here's three key moments from the podcast...
The first few months of 2026 were "the most terrifying" of his life

"In January, I started getting weird sensations - anxiety through the roof, insomnia began again, and then I started getting these weird pains. January, February, March was the most terrifying period of my life ever. It was like nothing I'd experienced, to the extreme that when I'd think about album release shows that we did, they were basically long panic attacks on stage. They were the worst."
He's been rebuilding his relationship with performing
"I used to believe that I only deserved to exist if I'm giving 100 percent on stage or off stage. You can't keep that up. It's ridiculous.

Now I'm trying this thing where you discipline yourself to just give 50% and that's it. You walk off stage and what it's doing is it's proving to you that life goes on. You exist, you still deserve to exist. People will still connect with you and appreciate you. Most people won't even notice a damn difference. And then you go, 'Oh, okay, I don't need to go through life giving my all all the time, or I won't be accepted.' It's almost like the shows aren't just shows now. They're actually an exercise in hopefully improving my mind."
As a companion to this podcast episode, we've made you a special playlist featuring lots of Shikari plus tunes from Fugazi, Refused, Blood Brothers, and more. Browse our playlist archive .
They're proud of the progress made with the grassroots levy
"To see that develop has been a joy. The surreal thing of hearing your name in the House of Lords is not what you'd ever expect.

"So yeah, it's been incredible. I will say at the same time, I suppose the bigger question is why does the music industry need an influx of money essentially, in order to stay afloat? It goes back to everything we've ever talked about.

"It's the fact that the music industry is an industry within a market-based capitalist economy, which means that power and wealth is always gonna consolidate into smaller and smaller monopolised areas, which brings all sorts of problems. And then you've got the incentives, not just the pure incentive of making art and human connection and bringing people together, which is what music has been since we were hunter gatherers around a campfire.

Nothing but Highlights: Is Power Slap the Sport We Deserve?
"Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance."

Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. But in an era of ever-shrinking attention spans, getting to the point (or the slap) within seconds seems to be the surest way to hold viewers. According to its founder, Dana White, “Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade.” Stuart McGurk deftly guides us through the rise of the slap, and talks with those who fear the consequences of hitting someone round the head as hard as you can.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or…
Around 210,000 carbon monoxide detectors are being recalled because they don't properly detect dangerous levels of carbon monoxide.

Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide , potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
What consumers need to know about the recall
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.

The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.

The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.

Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall , mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.
Consumers should continue using their recalled detectors until the replacement is installed. Once registration is confirmed, they should dispose of the recalled unit in their household trash.

For additional information, consumers can email recall@truststeadfast.com or visit the company’s recall website. Given the potential consequences, this is one recall homeowners won’t want to overlook.

Patrick Stewart’s health struggles made filming Avengers: Doomsday especially emotional

12 Common Holiday-Party Disasters—And How to Fix Them ASAP
From kitchen mishaps to awkward moments with guests, even the most carefully planned celebration can go awry. Here's how to keep your cool and save the day.

I entertain a lot around the holidays, and I mean a lot: an annual party with former work colleagues; a Hanukkah dinner (I’m not Jewish, but my crew love latkes); a homemade-pizza night and gingerbread-house-building session with my niece, her BFF and their moms; and, of course, the Feast of the Seven Fishes, the Italian American Christmas Eve tradition .

I’m a planner, and an incredibly organized one, at that. I’ve got spreadsheets with shopping lists, ingredient lists, detailed to-do lists … you get the picture. And yet, no matter how prepared I am, things happen. Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.

The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”

To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting , I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.

So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!

You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.

What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink , and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Grab a drink, and help me finish up!” is a perfectly acceptable response, says Rhinehart. My friends know that’s the case at my house: You show up early, and I’m putting you to work.

(For what it’s worth: Meier notes that guests should arrive at the stated time for a seated dinner; for a more casual gathering, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the start time is generally appropriate.)

Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!

You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.

What to do: Take a breath , pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”

Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.

Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”

Is It Really Rude to Opt Out of the Gift Exchange?
The anxiety—and financial pressure—of getting a present for a group gift swap can feel exhausting during an already overscheduled season. Can you just skip it? The post Is It Really Rude to…

Like all torturous extended family traditions, ours started with good intentions. One year, someone got left off the list during our chaotic annual Christmas gift free-for-all. Feelings were hurt. So being responsible adults, we fixed the problem by inventing an entire bureaucracy: the Official Family Gift Exchange.

The idea was fine. The rules were what ruined us. It started with just drawing names. Then we added a price limit. Then a price minimum, after somebody’s “gift” turned out to be an already-opened bottle of lotion. Then a rule requiring you to talk to your assigned person about their interests, which metastasized into a 15-question survey, then into a shared spreadsheet, tracked with the rigor of a Pentagon budget.

Then the “ no regifting ” clause. Then the Great Gift Card Debate, which raged for years: Do gift cards even count as real gifts? Does one to a specific store outrank a Visa card? Does it have to be taped to something ­wrappable, or are we now just handing each other receipts?

It all came to a head the year my husband’s gift got returned to him. Not regifted— returned, like a defective toaster , with a note that it wasn’t thoughtful enough. Being an eternal optimist, he tried again. That gift also came back, this time via USPS, meaning the recipient paid actual postage to send it away rather than keep it one more day. That’s when we knew we wanted out. It wasn’t working anymore.

My husband and I decided to pull the plug. No elaborate exchange, just a gift card to each family, no survey required. What had started as a fun, generous tradition had somehow turned into a monthlong hostage situation that began every November.

Naturally, quitting had consequences: The following year, someone anonymously (although I’m pretty sure I know who) sent us a calendar of dogs pooping. (Yes, that’s a thing. And yes, you can buy it. I do not recommend gifting it, though I also cannot stop thinking about the person who decided the world needed it as a wall calendar.)

It’s not just my family that has a hard time managing this. More often than not, gift exchanges—office, family or friend group—start as a fun idea but end up being a spreadsheet with hurt feelings. So is opting out of the whole enterprise actually rude?

Financially, gift exchanges have quietly inflated like everything else. A $10 white elephant gag gift is now a $25-and-up “guideline” that creeps to $40 the second someone brings a nice candle. Multiply that by the office exchange, the neighborhood exchange and the family swaps, and you’re out $200 before buying anything for someone you actually live with. And, it must be said, in this economy?

There are also the plain logistics: Exchanges take time most of us don’t have in December. Saying no to one more obligation isn’t a personality flaw; it’s functioning boundaries. And if the group’s response to “I’ll sit this one out” is outrage, that says more about their expectations than your manners.

If only it were that easy. Gift swaps, especially the family and friend kind, aren’t really about the gift. They’re a shared ritual , and rituals only work if everyone shows up. Opt out and you can shift the whole dynamic—an odd number of ornaments, a recalculated spreadsheet, or Grandma noticing the empty spot under the tree and asking about it at dinner, forever.

There’s also the momentum problem. Once one person opts out “just this year,” the tradition can quietly die. If the exchange genuinely matters to the group, your exit—however ­reasonable—can be the beginning of the end for people who looked forward to it.

Context is everything, and office, family and friend exchanges are not all the same animal. Office exchanges are the easiest to skip—it’s a workplace, not a family reunion, and “I’m sitting this one out” needs zero explanation. Unless, of course, your boss makes it mandatory.

In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined a falling lift in which people are performing experiments: One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch…
In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined a falling lift in which people are performing experiments :

One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:
‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.

‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Nothing can be heavy , you know, except by trying to fall, and being prevented from doing so. You all grant that?’

‘Well, now, if I take this book, and hold it out at arm’s length, of course I feel its weight . It is trying to fall, and I prevent it. And, if I let go, it falls to the floor. But, if we were all falling together, it couldn’t be trying to fall any quicker, you know: for, if I let go, what more could it do than fall? And, as my hand would be falling too — at the same rate — it would never leave it, for that would be to get ahead of it in the race. And it could never overtake the falling floor!’

Here’s How to Easily Record Your Entire Family History So No One Forgets Who’s Who in All Those Photos
Up to your eyeballs in old photos, letters and records? These expert tips to document your family history will help you organize everything and connect the dots.

My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
How do you create a family tree?
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.

If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.

How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.

This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study
A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

MFK Fisher’s clandestine campaign to spread Japanese cuisine and transform American food culture
This essay is co-published with Vittles and appears in Vittles Issue No. 3: The Influencers .
Vaughn Tan | Longreads | November 24, 2026 | 3,989 words (17 minutes)

Back in 2003, I was in the early stages of researching how the distinctive visual style of Japanese plating and dish design influenced plating outside Japan, and wanted to analyze photos of fine-dining dishes in industry periodicals like Art Culinaire . Back in the early 2000s, this was easiest to do in libraries. At the time, I lived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so I wound up in the collection of historical cookbooks and culinary materials at the Schlesinger Library.

A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

The American Red Cross is advising Americans to follow these easy safety rules in the kitchen this holiday season.

Simple Thanksgiving cooking habits can help prevent fires and hazards
It doesn’t take a major mistake for a fire to start. That’s what makes kitchen fires so sneaky and dangerous. Here are some safe-cooking tips to keep in mind this Thanksgiving.
Turn off the stove: The Red Cross recommends staying in the kitchen whenever you’re using the stovetop or oven. If you need to step away, even briefly, turn off the appliance first.
Avoid loose clothing: Be careful about what you’re wearing too. Loose clothing and dangling sleeves can easily catch fire.
Keep tabs on flammable items: Paper towels, oven mitts, wooden utensils, food packaging and curtains should stay away from hot appliances.
Establish a “safe cooking zone”: If you have children or pets, the Red Cross says to keep them at least three feet away from cooking areas.
Get a fire extinguisher: Be prepared for potential problems. Have a fire extinguisher nearby and know how to use it before an emergency happens.
One final safety note about frying turkeys

Thanksgiving and Christmas meals often feature turkeys, so turkey fryers deserve extra attention. Anyone preparing a fried turkey should keep the fryer outdoors, away from the house, garage and other structures. It should sit on a flat, stable surface, and the turkey must be completely thawed before it goes into the fryer.

Think about it: Katniss strikes back only when slighted first, like when she jabs the knife in the table when no one responds and when she shoots the arrow at the pig when she’s ignored. Then there’s a fact that you’re a little slow to do … everything . Katniss thinks things through and takes calculated risks, and she’s slow to open up, even to Peeta.
I originally picked Taurus for Katniss simply because it makes sense (and you know it!). But lo and behold, Katniss’s birthday is, in fact, on May 8, which means she’s a full-blooded Taurus!

You’re the chatterbox of the group, Gemini, which makes sense since you’re ruled by Mercury, the planet of communication and quick wit. As a television host, Caesar is basically a professional talker, and well, did we mention that you kind of love talking? You can literally spark a conversation with anyone and get them to open up. For Caesar, that means encouraging a shy girl like Rue to share her strengths, pumping up the ego of District 1’s socialites, and tugging on the heartstrings of every viewer in the Capitol—all within a five-minute segment.

Your other special talents include sarcasm, jokes and the tactical ability to change topics seamlessly when it’s uncomfortable. Caesar is exceptional at these things, which helps him avoid plenty of national, broadcasted disasters. Remember when he cut to commercial when Peeta brilliantly announced that Katniss was pregnant?

Hey folks. Like the rest of the internet & other tech infrastructure, KDO has seen some outages in the past week or so, amounting to a few hours of downtime. Our time here together isn’t what I would call mission critical — reading the site an hour or two after you’d originally wanted to is not the worst thing in the world — but it’s still a bummer to have the site be unavailable.

The reasons for the KDO downtime have been various, but that it occurred around the same time as some of these other outages isn’t, IMO, coincidental. Security researchers and developers armed with LLMs are going bananas finding exploits in a bunch of the software and infrastructure underpinning, well, everything. On the other side of the aisle, sysadmins are scrambling to fix all of these newly found exploits.

But of course, poking holes in things is easier & faster than plugging them. LLMs can help with the patching, 1 but it’s asymmetric warfare — being slow & careful with upgrades and patches isn’t a luxury you have when so many things are coming at you on a daily basis. Hopefully the situation won’t get too much worse before it gets better, but in the meantime, I’m thankful for everyone who is trying to keep these systems running. 🙏

Set two spheres against one another and wrap them in a third, as shown. Now add a new sphere, tangent to the first two and to the large enclosing sphere. Surprisingly, if you keep adding these new spheres, tangent to one another, they’ll always form a “necklace” of six.

English radiochemist Frederick Soddy discovered this pretty fact in 1937, though it had been known to Japanese mathematicians since at least 1822. Soddy, who had written a paean to Descartes’ theorem in Nature in June 1936, added another that December to celebrate his finding:
However ill-assorted in girth three spheres may be
Each one can kiss the other two simultaneously
A ring of six about them all kissing serially.
Though any necklet of graded beads
May fit in general the she-sex,
This hexlet of mine of novel design
Caresses not one but three necks.
However it’s worn it alters its grade
Whilst hugging three necks with precision.
Like bubbles that blow and kindle and go
It holds up to light-hearted derision
And its pet aversion in the mental inversion
All saints and sages throughout the ages
From one doxy never have swerved,
To hold fast unto what in change changes not
And ferret out what is conserved.
Now these beads without flaw obey this first law
For the aggregate sum of their bends.
As each in the tunnel slims through the funnel
But the mean of the bends of each opposite pair
Is the sum of the three of the thoroughfare.

How did Friday manage to leave a single footprint for Robinson Crusoe to discover?

I went up the shore, and down the shore, but it was all one; I could see no other impression but that one. I went to it again to see if there were any more, and to observe if it might not be my fancy; but there was no room for that, for there was exactly the very print of a foot — toes, heel, and every part of a foot. How it came thither I knew not, nor could in the least imagine.

“Was the single footprint made by some monstrous hopping cannibal?” asks John Sutherland in The Folio Book of Literary Puzzles (2007). “Perhaps Long John Silver passed by, from Treasure Island , with just the one foot and a peg leg? Has someone played a prank on Robinson Crusoe by raking over the sand as one does in a long-jump pit, leaving just the one ominous mark?”
(Strictly speaking Friday doesn’t appear until seven years after this episode, so possibly he didn’t leave the print. But someone did!)
