I don’t think it’s a surprise at this point when I tell you that I love these artworks by Antwerp-based artist Joost Vandebrug . (I mean, tell me they don’t aesthetically rhyme with the KDO logo circles/moons…)

Joost Vandebrug explores how separate views and moments come to be seen as a whole. His landscapes gather fragments into places that feel familiar, even when no single place could contain them. The image takes shape through remembering and looking, while the joins keep its construction visible.

Each work is built from dozens of photo-emulsion transfers on handmade paper cards. I transfer and reassemble them individually. Nothing is ever the same — every card has its imperfections. When I lay them together, they form a new landscape — part remembered, part reinvented.

Yeah, I love everything about this — the chunky pointillism, analog pixel art, small multiples, even Magic the Gathering vibes (if you think of the artworks as playable decks). Check out more of his work on his website and Instagram . Thanks to my pal Yen for the intro to his work; she snapped a photo of Vandebrug’s work in a gallery she visited recently.
"As Americans live longer than ever, car crashes involving elderly adults are on the rise. The question is what to do about it—and how many more deadly accidents it will take for us to act."

Americans are living longer these days, long enough to become vehicular terrors behind the wheel in their eighties and nineties, and they’re injuring themselves and others at unprecedented rates. David Howard, with additional reporting from Lloyd Alter, does the math and suggests that simply taking a senior’s licence away is not the answer; America is car-centric and many seniors need to drive in order to grocery shop, attend health appointments, and to meet their social needs. Could autonomous vehicles provide the balance we need between safety and independence?

Already visible on the technological horizon, of course, are self-driving cars, which carry the potential to obviate many of the limitations older drivers face. Mark Needham (not his real name) lives on the fringes of Charlottesville, Virgina. He is 82 and still active: He practices yoga at a local health club, engages in a glassblowing hobby, and dabbles with technology. He and his wife, 80, have lived in the same subdivision for 40 years, and while she’s wrestling with several health issues and is ready to move into a retirement facility, he’s adamantly opposed to it. “My wife is more inclined to being taken care of,” Needham says.
“I’m more inclined to be doing stuff.”

Part of what allows him to maintain his independence: a Tesla that over his two-plus years of ownership has morphed, via a steady stream of software updates, into a largely autonomous vehicle. (Many reviewers and experts still cite the need for improvement with tasks like changing speeds and parking before use becomes widespread.) “It drives better than I drove 30 or 40 years ago,” he says.

Founded in 1856 as the Palais de la Nouveauté, Dufayel became one of the world’s largest department stores, famous for selling furniture and household goods on credit. At its height, the business employed approximately 15,000 people.
The store closed in 1930. The premises subsequently became offices, notably for BNP, before their latest transformation.

The former Grands Magasins Dufayel in Paris’s 18th arrondissement has recently undergone a major restoration and conversion into a modern office complex called WOW. As of November 2026, the redevelopment is substantially complete, but the property is no longer a department store or public shopping destination. It is being marketed as premium commercial office space.

The staircase, a sweeping, bifurcated stair with ornate iron balustrades, one of the most theatrical interior features of Dufayel, is one of the key historic elements that has allegedly survived. The catch is that, like the rest of the converted interior, it is now inside a private office building, so it is not normally open to the public for visits. The recent redevelopment states that the “escalier patrimonial” / historic staircase was restored, alongside the façade and the Eiffel-style metal structure, rather than removed. VINCI Immobilier likewise says the project aimed to preserve notable elements including the stairs and part of the original floors while modernizing the building for office use.

Recent descriptions of the completed WOW project say that this historic staircase was renovated “à l’identique” — essentially restored in kind — and remains at the heart of the building. But I’ve yet to see any photographic evidence of that and I have serious doubts, though the staircase was perhaps lost long before current redevelopments took shape. A challenge for some Paris-based sleuths to confirm?! If I have time this week, I may pop out of the shop myself to check.

From Gandhi to Gen Z: A Century of Protest
India’s latest student-led demonstrations are part of a long tradition of political resistance that has shaped the nation’s democracy.

Gen Z protests in India in July demanded the resignation of the Minister for Education following a string of student suicides. The deaths followed the cancellation of a medical training examination after its exam paper was leaked. After millions engaged in peaceful protests throughout the country, the minister eventually resigned.

After a brief hiatus, the protests regained momentum following news that the election commissioner, who oversees the independent body responsible for conducting elections at both central and state levels, was accused of deleting thousands of names of eligible voters from electoral lists on the basis of their religion. Some parties claim that this has affected the outcome of elections across the country in favor of the Hindutva groups currently in power.

While the increased level of participation in these protests may seem surprising after years of citizens tolerating an increasingly fascist state apparatus, India has a long history of peaceful protests to bring about change.

Mahatma Gandhi’s non-violent movements, which began 100 years ago, brought the mighty British Empire to heel. “Under the inspiring leadership of Gandhi, several movements were launched to pinpoint the urgency and need for granting independence to India,” writes Dalip Singh in his paper “ Protest Movements in India ,” published in The Indian Journal of Political Science in 1991. These movements took place in phases, including the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920 – 21, the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930 – 31, the Individual Disobedience Movement of 1940, and the Quit India Movement of 1942 – 45. The underlying principle common to all these movements, however, was non-violence. Singh writes, “Even those followers of Gandhi who did not believe in non-violence as a creed, accepted it as a political expediency. From the above account one has to accept that hunger strike, bandh, gherao, dharna, etc. had gained the legitimacy of the people during the nationalist movement.”
Published seventy-five year ago, Amrita Pritam’s Pinjar explores the devastation suffered by the women of India and Pakistan after political rupture.

This system, termed the “ Gandhian system of protest ” by retired professor Chaman Lal, was lauded in an article published in the Economic and Political Weekly in 2016. He wrote of a gathering of writers and activists on the eighty-sixth anniversary of the historic Dandi March to “raise their voice against growing communal aggression against innocent people, not only in India, but throughout the world.”

David H. Bayley, meanwhile, divides the systems of protest in India into two distinct categories in a 1969 paper published in Pacific Affairs titled “ Public Protest and the Political Process in India ,” calling them legal and illegal forms of protest. The illegal forms come in two varieties—violent and nonviolent. Satyagraha, or nonviolent civil disobedience, is a nonviolent but often illegal form of protest. Violent illegal protest refers primarily to riots, although it may include assassinations and coups d’état as well. Bayley explains the political motivation for such violence:: “The point to underscore is that one common variety of social violence in Modern India has an explicitly political motivation, and it stems from a desire to shape government policy.” This, however, also seems to be the case with recent nonviolent protests.

Listen to the Music of the Ancient World: From 40,000-Year-Old Flutes to Ancient Greek Songs
There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit…

There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above , Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind previously featured here on Open Culture ) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese bianzhong bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.

Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader
"A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader."
“A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H.P. Lovecraft advised aspiring writers . We’ve already seen that reading is a learned skill and an optimizable technique , and that non-reading is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a good reader?

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life . He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected Lectures on Literature ( public library ), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:
Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:
The reader should belong to a book club.
The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
The reader should be a budding author.
The reader should have a dictionary.
The reader should have some artistic sense.

The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.
He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Friday essay: What if …? The imaginative adventure of reading alternative histories
An interest in alternative histories is shared by novelists and historians. Yet they pursue quite different aims.

Regime Change , Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s account of the first year of Donald Trump’s historically unprecedented return to the United States presidency, begins with an intriguing detour. For several pages, the authors imagine an alternative history in which Trump won re-election in 2020 and commenced his second term in 2021 rather than 2025.

In this scenario, Trump emerges from his first administration more cautious and constrained, lacking the opportunity to galvanise supporters through claims of electoral theft and political persecution. As a result, the upheavals that characterised his eventual return to office never occur. Had the 2020 election produced a different result, Haberman and Swan speculate, we might now be living in a calmer and more predictable world.

This desire to consider alternative histories, how the world might have changed if a known event had a different outcome, is shared by novelists and historians. Yet they generally pursue different aims.
All approaches to alternative history begin with what writers and scholars often describe as a point of divergence: a plausible change to recorded events that could have created a different timeline.

The possibilities are almost endless. What if Adolf Hitler had been assassinated in 1943 rather than dying by suicide in 1945? What if the Soviet Union had reached the Moon before the US in 1969? What if smallpox had never devastated the Indigenous peoples of North America? What if Christopher Columbus had failed to reach the Americas in 1492, only for European societies to face an Incan invasion decades later?
From a single altered event, entirely different worlds may emerge.

Alternative history fiction is built upon this premise. This subgenre can be identified in literature as early as 1490. The chivalric romance Tirant lo Blanc tells the story of a wandering knight who manages to prevent the fall of Constantinople and the destruction of the Byzantine Empire.

But alternative histories really take off in the 19th and 20th centuries. Authors were drawn to imagine the unfamiliar realities that might have resulted from, for example, Napoleon’s successful conquest of Europe , or a Confederate victory in the American Civil War .

The history of the second world war, in particular, frequently invites this kind of speculation. Philip K. Dick’s classic The Man in the High Castle describes a US partitioned between Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan after the Axis powers triumph.
Robert Harris’ Fatherland similarly depicts a post-war Nazi regime, using the conventions of noir crime fiction to reveal the hidden atrocities of the German state, 20 years after its victory.
More recently, New Zealand author Catherine Chidgey, in her novel The Book of Guilt , has explored how an early, negotiated end to the war might have resulted in an uncannily different 1970s England.

Although often associated with science fiction, alternative history is difficult to confine to a single genre. It has attracted literary novelists , as well as fantasy , young adult and steampunk authors. Its appeal lies not just in historical speculation, but in the opportunity to consider how conditions of life might change in this altered reality and what this may reveal about our understandings of human nature, society and history.
Alternative history fiction is often treated as a relatively contemporary form of speculation and storytelling. But the practice goes back to the entangled origins of literary and historical writing.

The roots of alternative history can be traced to Herodotus, whose Histories are regarded as foundational texts of the Western historical tradition. In addition to their detailed accounts of the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian wars, they are notable for Herodotus’ explicit interest in providing explanations for the events he described.

Herodotus was arguably influenced by the storytelling traditions of his time and their preoccupation with divine fate and tragic inevitability. He describes a world where acts of kindness are met with gratitude, and wrongs are violently avenged. What results is a conception of history as a causal…
How Did Thanksgiving Become a National Holiday?
If you happen to have ever wondered how Thanksgiving became a national holiday in the U.S., this was largely thanks to the author of Mary Had a Little Lamb, Sarah Hale. Hale was insanely…

If you happen to have ever wondered how Thanksgiving became a national holiday in the U.S., this was largely thanks to the author of Mary Had a Little Lamb, Sarah Hale. Hale was insanely influential in just about every facet of American life from architecture to how people dressed to even helping to launch the careers of many American authors, including Edgar Allen Poe.

Here is an excerpt covering all this from my soon to be published book Quincy: The Story of America. If you’re interested in checking the book out, you can sign up to be notified when it launches here

Born in New Hampshire shortly after the American Revolution to war veteran Captain Gordon Buell and his wife Martha, Sarah Josepha Hale’s otherwise relatively humble origins would belie her future massive influence on the United States. Critical for all this, Hale’s parents believed women should be educated and saw to it that she was, with her mother homeschooling her and her brother Horatio. Hale wrote of this in 1837, “I owe my early predilection for literary pursuits to the teaching and example of my mother. She had enjoyed uncommon advantages of education for a female of her times – possessed a mind clear as rock-water, and a most happy talent of communicating knowledge.”

This continued until it was time for her brother to attend a college, in this case Dartmouth, something that wasn’t an option for her. Her education nonetheless continued as she states, “[Horatio] seemed very unwilling that I should be deprived of all his collegiate advantages.”

Thus, after his classes were done each day, he would come home and go over everything he’d learned with his sister and then they’d proceed to study together. The culmination of this education was not only Horatio graduating from Dartmouth, but him awarding Sarah a diploma from the Horatio Gates Buell College, decreeing she’d graduated Summa Cum Laude with a degree in the Arts.

Much like another chief female character in the story of America, Abigail Adams, Sarah’s insatiable love of learning continued throughout her life, and was reciprocated and supported by her eventual husband, lawyer David Hale, whom she married in 1813 at the age of 25.

Hale describes her and her husband’s evening home life, “We commenced, soon after our marriage, a system of study and reading which we pursued while he lived. The hours allowed were from eight o’clock in the evening till ten; two hours in the twenty-four: how I enjoyed those hours! In all our mental pursuits, it seemed the aim of my husband to enlighten my reason… strengthen my judgment, and give me confidence in my own powers of mind, which he estimated much higher than I.”
The two would even help form a literary club where she took her first steps towards becoming a published author.

Unfortunately for the couple, David Hale died of pneumonia in 1822. Despite later becoming something of the queen of dictating fashion in the United States, from her husband’s death for the final 57 years of her life, Hale wore black clothing in perpetual mourning over the loss of her partner.

In the immediate upon his death, she was left with trying to figure out how to support herself and the couple’s five children, the fifth of which was born just two weeks after David’s death, all in an era where lucrative jobs for women were virtually non-existent.

Hale had previously spent time as a teacher, but resuming that profession wouldn’t have been sufficient to support her family, so, with the help of her deceased husband’s Masonic friends and her sister-in-law, she started a business making and selling hats for women.

But as for her long term plan, she elaborated that as there were “very few employments in which females can engage with any hope of profit… my own constitution and pursuits made literature appear my best resource.”

As such, she began writing in earnest, including successfully selling pieces she’d authored to various magazines such as the American Monthly, Minerva, and New York Mirror. On top of this, also with the help of the Free Masons, she published a book of poems called The Genius of Oblivion and Other Original Poems.
The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love
"Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment."
“Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment.”

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on why we fall and how we stay in love . “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist Donald Hall (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of Poetry — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in “the bead of sensation” that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker . The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do? ”

What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing Little Prince author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s beautiful insistence that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.
For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach…
For centuries, lost cargo sparked fierce battles over who had the right to claim treasures washed ashore.

In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships , so huge they were referred to as “ floating cities ,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.

The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage , the “right of wreck.”

It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”

That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord . In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)

Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling . Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).
Lonely Diarist of the High Seas
As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story.

The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee . Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.

In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “ man, dog, or cat ” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)

Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia , for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.
A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:

How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne. “I am convinced…

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne . “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it . “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in a more recent Smithsonian piece . (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is an original Swanson TV dinner tray .) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

The Illustrated Version of “Alice’s Restaurant”: Watch Arlo Guthrie’s Thanksgiving Counterculture Classic
Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter…

Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein , arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post .) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”
We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes
Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with…

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable , that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop , the golden fan of the gingko , the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe .
In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).
— in this dim parade of brutality —
But if we trouble it with light,
So love the thousand knives as they enter
and see your shape still sitting.
See that you too belong to paws
of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled
Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.
The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.
in this world we’re pressed into,
For what we build, speak, and ruin —

“The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself . And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness , completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry ( public library ) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society .

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.
In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming , Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change , then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit .

250 years ago, as the leaves changed and the weather turned colder, General George Washington and the Continental Army marched across Pennsylvania and New Jersey. In the evenings, Washington retreated to his marquee tents, which served as both the center of field command and the general’s private quarters. Through the rain and the ice, Washington camped under a canopy made of linen—trusty, waterproof, and American-made .

In the 1760s, as taxes on British imported goods rose under King George III (r. 1760–1820), American colonists turned to homespun textiles as symbols of resistance and ultimately, independence. One of these textiles was linen , spun and woven from the fibers of the flax plant. Washington’s tent was made by a Pennsylvania upholsterer rather than in private homes, but for women, spinning bees and weaving contests became a way of participating in Revolutionary activities while navigating complex gender dynamics. While cotton is king in the history of American textiles, flax played an important role in the cultural front of the American Revolution, uniting soon-to-be Americans in industriousness and self-sufficiency.

Flax, or Linum usitatissimum , is one of the oldest continuously cultivated plants in the world , with fibers discovered in the Alps dating back to 5000 BCE . It typically grows in sandy loam and temperate climates, creating blankets of slender stalks and blue flowers in the springtime. Flaxseeds can be ground and eaten or pressed into flaxseed oil or linseed oil . The former is edible and rich in mega-3s, and the latter is used in commodities ranging from paints to linoleum (a material named after the words “linen” and “oil”). But far and away, the most common use of flax is to create the durable, breathable textile—linen.

In ancient Egypt, linen made from flax was ubiquitous , appearing in everything from mummy wrappings to everyday attire. It quickly spread to Europe and beyond. In 789, the future emperor Charlemagne decreed that all households should cultivate their own flax and produce domestic textiles at home.

By the seventeenth century, the weaving of linen was a skilled craft in Europe. Peasants would typically grow, process, and spin their own flax yarn and then bring it to a local artisan— who was usually male —to weave into cloth. As the colonial world expanded, so did the linen trade. Both the Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company had unsuccessfully encouraged settlers at Jamestown and Massachusetts to cultivate flax in the early seventeenth century , but later efforts to grow the crop in North America succeeded. Linen plants were soon growing up and down the East Coast, along with the most productive colonies in the mid-Atlantic region.

In seventeenth-century North America, women spun thread but did not weave ; weaving was considered a skilled craft that only a man could hone and monetize. However, by the mid-eighteenth century, the gender norms of linen production were changing. The economy of the thirteen colonies developed rapidly, with complex networks of trade connecting the settlers to mainland England and beyond. Despite the common misconception of early American self-sufficiency, the average colonist spent more than one-quarter of their budget on imports .

Even so, they were no strangers to taxation that caused shockwaves in the homegrown textile economy. The Wool Act of 1699 prevented colonists from exporting their wool to protect the English textile industry. Weaving became a way for daughters to contribute wealth to the household at a time when it was unseemly for them to work in the field or accept wages. As historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich writes, the development of weaving among American women was “ neither an artifact of rural poverty nor a response to frontier exigency. It was a colonial adaptation to an expanding mercantile economy .” By the 1770s, the American textile industry was developing rapidly. As such, the act of turning flax into usable textile products became part of the daily lives of women, who, as Ulrich explains, “ measured their days, not in coffee spoons, but in knots and skeins .”

Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir An Unexpected Life , published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, An Unexpected Life is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s . “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in An Unexpected Life , a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of Ms. Magazine in 1971. The Radicalization of Eugene V. Debs and the Country He Radicalized in Return
On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House.

On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House. Just shy of twenty-two years old, he’d been a member of his labor union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, for barely two and a half years. But today he would deliver the opening address to its national convention.

Horse-drawn wagons and carriages rolled through the downtown streets of Indianapolis, clacking on the cobblestones and kicking up gravel as paved stretches came to an end. Lavishly ornamented cast-iron buildings mingled with simple brick structures; steam whistles sounded from the railroad tracks bound for the teeming Union Depot, the first in the country to bring all train traffic to a central hub. City leaders were thinking longterm here. Meatpacking was the city’s other big industry, Kingan and Company’s mammoth plant one of the largest in the world, its state-of-the-art chilling system allowing year-round production in these days before refrigeration.

Indianapolis wasn’t Chicago or St. Louis, Midwestern metropolises with populations in the hundreds of thousands, but its 75,000 inhabitants painted a smaller-scale picture of a rapidly industrializing America. With all the corresponding possibilities and cruelties. The boom-and-bust of capitalism had gone bust four years before in the so-called Panic of 1873, an economic disaster nearly as severe as the Great Depression of the 1930s—and joblessness persisted in Indianapolis, as elsewhere. Workers terrified of being laid off grudgingly accepted wage cuts. Politicians responded to calls for a public jobs program with creative new punishments instead: fines for begging, a proposed workhouse “where all persons incapable of paying fines” would be forced to smash stones to pave more city streets.

Soon, Gene Debs would have seen the Indiana State House come into view. A white wooden fence edged the tree-lined lawn—the trunks like matchsticks, branches draped with green leaves holding on despite the imminent change in seasons. The dome of the state capitol rose above, a grand if crumbling structure of blue limestone and gray stuccoed columns patterned on the Greek Parthenon. Debs—amiable and outgoing, a bit over six feet tall, with a slim but solid build—entered the capitol and mounted the stairs to the House of Representatives’ chamber on the upper floor, which the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was borrowing for the convention. He greeted his fellow delegates, who had exchanged their soot-stained work clothes for suits and ties.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work. Firemen shoveled the coal that powered steam engines into the locomotive’s firebox, which was prone to explosion. Every month the firemen’s magazine carried grim news of widowed wives, orphaned children, maimed railroaders. Train derailments and collisions were ubiquitous. Railroad workers made up the bulk of workplace injuries in Gilded Age America: by one count 56 percent of the broken ribs, 50 percent of broken arms, 41 percent of broken legs, 71 percent of severed arms, and all of the amputated legs.

Nearly one in four trainmen could expect to die on the job if he worked for thirty years; only coal mining was as lethal. The work was well paid by the standards of the day, with veteran engineers often able to own their own home, but shifts were long and irregular, running anywhere from twelve to twenty-four hours, or longer. “It is no uncommon thing,” one railroader said, “for an engineer to go for nearly a week without sleep except in snatches on the road or waiting on a branch or engine house.” Workers lived close to the railyards, knowing that at a moment’s notice they could be gone for days or weeks. The imperatives of their employers, rather than their own individual wants or collective needs, governed workers’ lives.

Not that Debs begrudged the railroad companies. If the work was too dangerous or too demanding, the hours too long or the bosses too harsh, it was up to railroad workers to prove themselves worthy of more respect. The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great…
Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science. Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology, physics, chemistry…

Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science . Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology , physics , chemistry , quantum physics , quantum computing , fungi , and many others besides. But with his latest map, Domain of Science creator Dominic Walliman has turned away from the scientific realm — or rather, he’s ventured into the larger intellectual territory out of which it emerged. His new Map of Philosophy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiquity like Thales, Laozi, Confucius, and the Buddha, who lived and died before science as we know it.

That hardly means that they’ve become irrelevant today. There still exist societies described as Confucian or Buddhist, of course, but in the Western world, we’re more likely to refer back to — and, in many cases, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. “They basically laid the intellectual foundation of Western philosophy, science, and political thought,” says Walliman. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unexamined life is not worth living, which “hits pretty hard in the age of the distraction economy.”)

Though often mentioned together, these three ancient Greeks occupy slightly different positions on the philosophical map, with Socrates closer to the land of ethics, Plato to metaphysics, and Aristotle to epistemology.

As Walliman explains, “epistemology studies knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it differs from faith or opinions,” while also seeking out its limits. Aristotle’s rigor in testing and organizing knowledge makes him, in a sense, one of the earliest scientists. Though his body of theory may no longer be our best means of understanding how the world works, his systematic pursuit of such an understanding set him apart from much of the ancient intellectual world. The islands off the coast of the map’s mainland represent subfields still actively explored today, like the philosophies of mind, language, politics, religion, and science — which, for all its prestige, remains as subject to philosophical inquiry as any other area of human endeavor. The map of philosophy shows us not a rarefied, mostly abandoned territory, but the place where we all live our lives, examined or otherwise.

Fingers, frozen to the bone in the damp cold, barely obey.

A trembling hand fumbles in the scratchy wool of an overcoat pocket for another five-round clip. That damned bolt again. The last round stuck fast. One strike. Another—with a numb palm. New clip…stiff bolt handle forward and down…chamber a new round and close the breech.
So cold. Eyes ache from peering into the fogged dark. The head throbs from gunfire crackling since morning.
A minor railway stop, Kruty, lost in bleak fields, near a nameless hamlet beyond Nizhyn.

“They’re coming, still coming, stay alert!” officers shout hoarsely from the snow-covered embankment, voices strained. Through icy fog and under the dim light of a veiled moon, shadows advance across the wide field, cut through by endless rails.
The Reds send another wave into the attack.
A flash splits the darkness on the far horizon. Then a boom, and an explosion close by. The blasts throb like a pulse in the temples.
Teeth clench. The head pulls inward, wishing never to hear and see, shrapnel whistles overhead. This time for sure.
A hoarse shout—the machine guns burst to life, tearing the darkness with short volleys, chewing through belts of cartridges.
Around, thin lines of defense stretch across the silvery ribbon of rails: a motley battalion of whoever God sent, in whatever they had, with God knows-what instead of proper weapons.

Students from Kyiv. Young cadets in old overcoats, in felt boots, with grimy yellow-blue armbands on their sleeves. Gymnasium students, mere schoolboys who had hardly ever fired a shot before, in ordinary clothes, standing off to the left to keep away from harm. Fiery, dreamy lads who did not run, too ashamed to turn their backs.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.

One student—his face still untouched by a razor—keeps nervously adjusting his round spectacles again and again, brushing frost-dust with trembling fingers. They had all volunteered. Shivering in the cold, breathing heavily. Clumsily digging shallow trenches. They weren’t meant to be here. Schoolboys, maybe good enough to haul ammo, nothing more. So they were sent to a “relatively quiet sector” of the front, but ended up encountering the main enemy forces.

A handful of junior officers, none over thirty, stand beside them in Russian army uniforms, their epaulets torn off, imperial cockades missing. This was the young army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic—its most devoted part.
“Matviy, keep an eye on the youngsters here!” A gloved hand claps his shoulder, and the officer ducks low, moving on to steady the thin line.

Another deep, dull thud, one that rings sharp in the skull, not just the ears. The soft stubble of a cheek touches the frozen wooden stock again. Lungs pull in frost. Another shot into the darkness merges into the deafening cannonade. And another. And again.

They keep coming with bayonets fixed, advancing toward the machine guns across the field to the station. Navy peacoats, quilted jackets, caps, red armbands. They’ve been coming since morning. Sailors of the Baltic Fleet. Red Guards from Petrograd and Moscow…no strangers to this kind of work.
There they lie, bastards. Dozens of black mounds, sprawled in the dark after a day of relentless charges—frozen mid-agony, a bullet still in the gut.
The Reds are advancing on Kyiv.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.
Kharkiv is lost, Poltava is lost, Chernihiv is lost. Through forests and steppe, along rails from Russia, the armored trains grind toward the Ukrainian capital.
Another heavy blow from the Bolshevik battery—and now they’re pulling him away: sotnyk Omelchenko, the student company leader, his head torn open by shrapnel, blood gushing from beneath his cap.
You won’t make it to Kyiv, friend. Remember us up there.
We can’t hold this alone. Not for long.
Finding My Way in the Wilderness with Brush and Pen
In 1994, as a refugee from New York City advertising (an accidental career resulting from a failed attempt to convert my biology degree into artistic fame in the big city), I returned to my…

In 1994, as a refugee from New York City advertising (an accidental career resulting from a failed attempt to convert my biology degree into artistic fame in the big city), I returned to my home state of Vermont and dove headlong into wildlife art, crisscrossing the U.S. for six years on the national art show circuit. I didn’t write anything but birthday cards to my daughters.

Right in the middle of a show out west in the winter of 2000/2001, it hit me: I’d become as much a teamster as an artist, and I felt cut off from what inspired me to paint. I ditched my late summer schedule and planned an August/September, 330-mile “source-to-salt” canoe trip on the Missinaibi River, which flows north to James Bay (I bought my first canoe with my paper route money when I was 11). The trip wasn’t to be an escapist adventure, but work: a painting trip and a chance to reconnect with my Muse, as a classicist would say.

It also introduced writing into my creative repertoire. Realizing that hardly anyone would notice if I disappeared into the wilderness for a month, I contacted an art magazine that liked the artist-on-a-canoe-trip angle, and a canoeing magazine that liked the canoeist-on-an-art-trip angle. I wasn’t sure what I would write, but I figured something would come to mind on the river.

I’d assumed I’d have to go alone with an artist’s itinerary, but at an art show opening in June, John Pitcher, a pre-eminent U.S. wildlife artist, asked to join me. On the river, John and I became fast friends and discussed future trips, but in Mattice, Ontario, after 130 miles, he had to return, and I continued solo.

As soon as Mattice disappeared behind a bend, the enormity of what I was doing settled in. I was alone, facing 200 miles of wild river through roadless wilderness. On the one hand, I was keenly aware that without anyone to help, even a minor mishap could cascade into tragedy. On the other, the river held my undivided attention.
The wild expanses I have experienced aren’t alien places, but reminders that the wild is where we all come from.

That first night alone, I camped at the Kettle Falls portage, and in a substantial blow to my self-image as an adventurer, I was hit with an acute attack of loneliness. I focused on setting camp and starting dinner, but I couldn’t shake the intense melancholy. Then the westering sun lit the river’s east bank with an evening glow. Hoping for another distraction, I set to painting while my dinner boiled. I had to work fast to catch the light, but before long (and to my pleasant surprise), the painting started to come alive. A surge of euphoria welled up out of nowhere and washed the loneliness away in a tidal wave so intense that, for a few moments, I wondered if I was OK. The weirdest part was a heartwarming sense of connection, not just to my surroundings, but to people—not anyone in particular, but everyone. I was never lonely on the river again.

That evening, as I dutifully recorded the day’s events in the journal the magazines had asked me to keep, I discovered that my new assignment was more than just a travelogue. The small painting that had precipitated one of the most intense emotional reactions of my life could, ironically, do nothing to describe or explain the internal transformation I’d undergone. But writing could.
The Way North – Kettle Falls, Missinaibi River . Acrylic field painting, September 4, 2001.

Over the next week, I made friends with Canada Jays and sandpipers, talked to rocks and various pieces of my gear, all of whom were generally supportive. On the other hand, an oblivious bull moose nearly killed me by accident, and a large bear looked like he was contemplating doing it on purpose.

But the river and forest offered only indifference. There was sound: birds, wind, the current along my hull or surging through rapids, but no noise and nothing I did seemed to matter. The ageless enormity of the planet pressed in, a wild Earth utterly unconcerned with humans, and as I thought back on the dizzying diversity of life that “Mother Earth” has birthed, provided for, and let pass away through the eons, I realized she is an impassive parent. “If sports novels are usually about greatness, erotica is usually about power. In Amazons , this calculation is simple: Cleo has it all. There is none of the usual give-and-take, no real battle of the sexes on the ice or in bed. That she can skate with the boys is never in question, and not a source of particular stress. “We may have queer culture to thank for the very fact that we’re reading Amazons in the first place. The Times report ed that DeLillo decided to reissue the book amid the buzz around Heated Rivalry and the clamor for hockey erotica. I would prefer not to believe this, because the rather lofty DeLillo of my imagination would never change his mind about a disowned book for such crassly commercial reasons. A major subplot of Amazons involves Cleo refusing to do an ad for a snack food because she prefers a different brand in real life. We are supposed to find this silly but righteous. Still, whatever made DeLillo reissue the book, I’m glad he did. Amazons is so bouncy, so immediately and frankly pleasurable to read, that it could be studied as an example of a book with no payoff which nevertheless leaves the reader satisfied. Amazons won’t teach you anything about womanhood or greatness or hockey, and will teach you only very little about various forms of male longing, an already overexplored subject. But perhaps that’s enough. As this accomplished sports novelist famously put it, ‘Longing on a large scale is what makes history.’”
–S. C. Cornell on Don DeLillo’s Amazons ( The New Yorker )

The Natural History of the Sea-Serpent

A lively review by Dr. Octavia Arbogad of The Natural History of the Sea Serpent, To which is added, a Sketch of a Serpent-Hunting Voyage , by Achabbu Zarxas, translated by Kailung Smirtha. Published in Koot-Hoomi’s Quarterly, New Lovegain, 1341.

The patron who does us the honor to take up this article, as a gentle preparative for an after-dinner nap, may, perhaps, pardon us for reminding them that the soft turquoise light of their sitting-room lamp is borrowed from the largest and most ferocious of known creatures; that the oil which turns night into day, and invests its power upon the steam-engines of our manufactories and rail-roads, once formed part of a vast and fearsome being whose heart sent out twenty or thirty gallons of blood at every stroke, through an aorta measuring more than two feet in diameter; and that the creature whose gigantic frame was nourished by this flood of life gamboled on the broad back of the World-Ocean, rejoicing in its strength, till the minuscule, mortal human, whose engines had grown hungry for the wyrms’ treacly ichor, made war upon the beast in its own realm, and left the enormous mass inanimate. Nor is every one acquainted with the dangers and privations borne by those who seek the terrible monster in its remote watery demesne. A serpent-hunting voyage often exceeds three years, and hardly ever occupies less than two. From the port of New Lovegain alone an average of seventy sail of fine ships, of a burthen ranging from three to four hundred tons, are annually on the look-out for the fattest of sea-serpents. The crews of these ships, which are fully provisioned for three years, and sail from New Lovegain at all times of the year, consist of from twenty-eight to thirty-three sailors and officers—including at least one sorcerer, typically a tempestarius also serving as navigational astrologer, which, after all, seems to us to be a very commendable species of mixed practice. As, for obvious reasons, there are in such expeditions “no more cats than can catch mice,” the mariner who has been afloat in one of these ships is pretty sure to turn out a crack specimen of their genus—a smart character, case-hardened to any climate, expert in all their professional duties—endued with imperturbable nerves and quick decision, eagle-eyed, and tyger-hearted.

All the sailors are, in point of fact, co-adventurers with the owner; for they go “on the lay”—that is, they have a certain share of the produce, instead of the ordinary money-payment. This arrangement, which sailors find eminently favorable to employment in the smoky labyrinths of New Lovegain’s rail-fed manufactories, can be ascribed to the influence of the Mazuraa cultus, particularly those clades which favor the worship of the Deep Goddess in Her incarnation as Gykylyk, Mother of Storms. Such teachings have long argued that the great serpents, being ex nihilo and tempore ruinae the creation of their favored goddess, therefore exist as the common property of humankind, who have worked for over a millennium to appease the deities’ displeasure. The rewards of the serpents’ oil, the sea-laborers have proclaimed, should then at least be shared equitably amongst the crew who procured the stuff.

The zeal with which this dangerous sea-hunt is pursued seems to take the strongest possession of the sailors’ minds; and one of their most usual modes of making a heavy hour light is sketching their favorite ship, serpents in various attitudes, and the hair-breadth escapes of their companions and themselves, upon the tooth or bone of one of the monsters whom they have seen die. One of the grandest examples of such craft I have seen was upon a ship that patrolled the waters between the southern New Lands and San Borondon, executed upon a yard-long tooth. Its panoramic image was of the fearsome creature from which it was plucked, pictured “in a flurry” and pursued by a spate of skiffs from a finely-detailed schooner, but pierced with almost as many darts as the fabled Archemedon Wyrm slain by the sea-monks of San Borondon in Ontic antiquity. Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.
What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life , “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:
Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.
When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.
The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself . Pärt puts it more gently:
One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.
If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.
I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:
Silence with you is like the faint delicious
Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:
Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,
The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.
Silence with you is like a kind departure
From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd
Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,
Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;
Or like one held upon the sands at evening,
When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light
Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed
Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

A self is a forest . A self is a ship . A self is an illusion , and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves , contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life , takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman ( public library | free ebook ).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma .)
In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
who would rebel against this madman.
Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
who would protest against serving this madman.
Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
