How Humans Are Helping Golden Jackals Conquer Europe
By unintentionally protecting jackals from larger predators, people are aiding in the expansion of a remarkably adaptable canid.

The golden jackal isn’t always the color of gold; its coat ranges from creamy beige to a rusty brown with black striations. It is, however, living in a golden age—thanks in part to the ubiquity of humans.

Native to Eurasia, golden jackals in Europe have historically been confined to the southeastern tips of the continent, mainly the Balkan countries. Over the past century, though, Canis aureus has slowly started colonizing new areas of Europe, with a steep acceleration over the past two decades. Golden jackals are expanding their range, reaching as far west as Spain and as far north as the Arctic. Scientists say the expansion represents one of the most dramatic changes in the range of a species in today’s world. New research, including genetic analysis, is revealing what’s driving the jackal’s spread and the part people play in the animal’s success.

One factor that has contributed to golden jackals’ expansion is anthropogenic climate change, which has decreased snow cover and probably revealed more suitable canid habitat. The habitat fragmentation that comes with farming and urbanization is another likely influence, since golden jackals prefer a patchy environment. The species also adapts readily to human-altered landscapes and can disperse hundreds of kilometers in search of new habitat. And, not least of all, researchers suspect that humans cleared the way for them by extirpating wolves across much of Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.
“The fact that they did not have any competitor made it easier,” says Jennifer Hatlauf, a wildlife ecologist who manages the Golden Jackal Project in Austria .

Today, researchers estimate that around 150,000 golden jackals inhabit 23 European countries, populating a range that’s 46 percent bigger than it was in 2016 . But wolf populations are growing, too; Europe hosts roughly 23,000 wolves today, compared to an estimated 12,000 as recently as 2012.

To better understand how humans, a growing wolf population, and the expanding golden jackal population interact, Hatlauf and a large team of researchers collected and analyzed data on the presence of golden jackals from all around Europe between 2001 and 2017. The information mainly came from playback surveys: Researchers played a jackal call from a speaker and listened for the response of real jackals, identifying the presence of individuals. The team then paired this data with data on wolf and human presence.

Their recently published analysis shows that the presence of wolves is the main factor limiting the expansion of jackals—a result that strengthens the hypothesis that the decline of wolves in past centuries likely opened the door to the jackal expansion. The team also found that human settlements create a shield that deters wolves and offers a refuge for jackals.

The “human shield” hypothesis isn’t new. Researchers have long known that prey or smaller predators take advantage of human presence to escape large predators. For example, some bear mothers with cubs find refuge from adult male bears by moving close to human settlements, especially during the mating season, when the males would try to kill offspring. Prey animals, such as wild turkeys, also seem to find safety near human-inhabited areas.

In places where wolves are absent, the data shows, jackals tend to stay away from humans, likely to avoid deadly encounters with our species. But where wolves are rooted in the landscape, jackals remain within humans’ proximity. “The jackal is three times smaller, so there’s simply no chance for a jackal if you have a core area of wolf populations,” says Hatlauf. That same life strategy is probably going to apply in other areas that jackals will reach in the future as they expand even farther, she adds.

“The work is excellent,” says Luigi Boitani, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe, who wasn’t involved in the research. The idea that the wolf’s extirpation played a role in the jackal’s expansion and that human presence shapes the relationship between the two species has long crossed scientists’ minds, Boitani says, but no one was able to prove it with actual data until now.

Hummingbirds often use their bills for fighting, but some species’ outsized appendages are equally useful in finding food.

Despite their diminutive size and zany colors, many hummingbird species are downright ferocious when they encounter one another at a food source. That’s likely because of the demands of their lightning-fast metabolisms. In flight, a hummingbird may flap its wings 62 times per second, and some species have heart rates that top out at over 1,200 beats per minute. Hummingbirds’ small bodies have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and they lack insulating down, so they also lose heat quickly. They must consume two to three times’ their body weight per day in high-sugar flower nectar.

Given that flowers bloom only for a short while, that makes each meal more like a high-stakes operation than a companionable feast. Even at feeders with abundant nectar supplied by humans, hummers of both sexes often joust—chasing and stabbing at each other with long, sharp bills, among other aggressive tactics and displays. The shining sunbeam ( Aglaeactis cupripennis )—on the left in this image by conservation biologist and photographer Maxime Aliaga—is no exception. Researchers tracking the species in the Andes Mountains of Peru and Ecuador found that it regularly defended flowers within its territory from hummingbirds of both its own and other species, including sword-billed hummingbirds ( Ensifera ensifera ) like the one pictured on the right.

Sword-billed hummingbirds, for their part, aren’t slouches. They wield their beaks—which are longer than their bodies—exactly as their name suggests. But the primary purpose of the species’ outsized appendage may be to get food, rather than defend it.

Scientists believe that the sword-billed hummingbird’s unique morphology evolved in tandem with long-tubed passionflowers. That subgroup within the Passiflora genus, called Tacsonia , contains more than 60 species with flower nectar tubes 6 to 14 centimeters (2 to 5 inches) long. That’s a close match with the sword-billed hummingbird’s beak, which can reach up to 11 centimeters (4 inches). The birds and flowers also overlap in range, with 37 Tacsonia species pollinated exclusively by sword-billed hummingbirds. They are the only hummingbird species with the correct proportions to deposit pollen grains on the stigmas of these dangling, downward-opening flowers, poking into them from below to drink nectar.

In intact cloud forests, this highly specialized mutualism is a boon to both plants and pollinators. But in fragmented forests, it becomes a vulnerability: Research suggests that sword-billed hummingbirds don’t frequent deforested areas. Scientists speculate that may be partly because the long-tubed passionflowers that they observed in these zones often lose their nectar to “robber” species like bees, which drill into the flowers from the side, skipping pollination and draining the hummingbirds’ food source. With the connection to the passionflowers’ primary pollinator severed, at least four species of the plant have likely gone locally extinct in landscapes fragmented by forest-clearing. Those passionflower species that have evolved shorter nectar tubes, though, are more resilient. They can rely on other hummingbirds and bats for pollination, even when the habitat becomes less suitable for sword-billed hummingbirds.

Searching for a Bird Lost to Science
A researcher grapples with the value of his efforts to document a secretive species in Papua New Guinea.

Our luck turns during a smoke break. It is hot and dry for Papua New Guinea, and we are resting on the shoulder of a gravel road, bags and cardboard biscuit boxes scattered on limestone bedrock. The boxes, in rough shape from travel, are printed with a cartoon of a man named Henry Wopa, whose bulging muscles advertise that his eponymous product is enriched with vitamins and protein. This has made the brand a staple in parts of Melanesia where deforestation has hurt food security, including here on New Britain, an island four times the size of Puerto Rico that accounts for a majority of PNG’s raw log exports . Still, the biscuits are bland and difficult to swallow without coffee, which is running out. I am hungry, but not hungry enough for more Wopa. Instead, as my colleagues squat in broken shade rolling cigarettes, I scan the canopy, ragged from decades of selective logging.

There are 10 of us in total: six Sengseng-speaking Arawe and four outsiders, including me—an evolutionary biologist from Montana—gathered to search for a poorly known bird called the New Britain bronzewing ( Henicophaps foersteri ). This large, glimmering pigeon, endemic to its namesake island, was last confirmed alive through a specimen collected by ornithologist-turned-author Jared Diamond in 1972. The bronzewing has been seen occasionally in the years since but was never again collected and has never been photographed. This is cause for some concern. As Joe Wood, an expedition member who manages international conservation programs for the Toledo Zoo & Aquarium in Ohio, put it: “It would be nice to check in on it.”

But how, exactly, do you check in on a handful of shy birds in tens of thousands of square kilometers of forest? By asking around, to start. Jason Gregg, a graduate student in my lab at Montana State University and the expedition’s leader, has spent years thinking about how to incorporate local ecological knowledge into biodiversity surveys, along with spending many hours interviewing our Arawe crew members. About half say they’re familiar with the species—known locally as kau—but communicating across gulfs of language and culture about a bird of which there are no photographs is challenging. The night before, Thomas Sunamli, who is letting us stay on his land, explained that the bronzewing is common in disturbed habitat and feeds on the red, pine-cone-like flowers of a plant called shampoo ginger ( Zingiber zerumbet ). This contradicted our own limited understanding of the bird’s diet and need for old growth.

“It’s hard to imagine what they could be getting out of [those flowers],” Wood had said, frowning as he prodded a clump of shampoo ginger at the edge of camp. Since nectar is rarely an important part of a pigeon’s diet, I was inclined to agree.

Western methods for locating the bird have so far proven ineffective. A week of constant observation, camera trapping, and attempts to attract the bird by playing the call of its closest relative through a makeshift speaker we’ve dubbed the Bronzewing Blaster 5000 have amounted to nothing. Nor is history in our favor. In the late 1950s, zoologists Thomas and Margaret Gilliard spent three months within a few dozen kilometers of our camp, collecting some 500 specimens representing 98 species for the American Museum of Natural History. Among their findings were two species new to science. Absent was a single bronzewing. To our knowledge, no ornithologists have visited here since.

The Gilliard expedition was one of the final episodes of a heyday of scientific exploration in Melanesia that had a profound influence on the fields of ecology and evolution, arguably birthing theories such as island biogeography . This era ended in 1975, when Papua New Guinea gained independence and ended colonial license to travel freely in a region that now has near-complete Indigenous land tenure. In the interim, logging corporations felled the last grand forests of Borneo and Sumatra and began working their way through New Britain. Today, cost, logistics, lack of infrastructure, and sporadic violent crime discourage many foreign biologists from studying how the logging is affecting the island’s biodiversity.

The world is full of tiny things that live off more charismatic hosts. Parasite ecologists say that these critters, too, are finally starting to get the conservation attention they deserve.
Hatchery-reared fish can help boost struggling populations, but fish raised in captivity are ill-prepared for life in the wild. Scientists have a plan to change that.

Douglas Tave likes to tell anyone who asks that there’s nothing special about the fish he has spent 20 years trying to save. “There is nothing special about the silvery minnow,” Tave repeats to me from the brown leather recliner in his desert home outside Albuquerque, New Mexico. “We get this question all the time.”

The Rio Grande silvery minnow ( Hybognathus amarus ) is a freshwater fish about the length of your pinky that has been stalled on the federal endangered species list since 1994. It is neither a symbiotic partner of another creature, nor an ecologically important parasite. It is not an apex predator in the river. Nor is it an irreplaceable prey. The silvery minnow isn’t even the only fish of its size in the Middle Rio Grande watershed, Tave tells me matter-of-factly. And it sure as hell isn’t the only endangered species there either. The New Mexico meadow jumping mouse, the southwestern willow flycatcher, and the Mexican wolf have all historically dwindled in the Albuquerque area. But Tave is a fish aquaculturist. He has studied fish hatcheries since the 1980s. And beneath the nonchalance is a rebellious humor seasoned by decades of championing controversial scientific ideas in state government.

“All you do is write papers that cause trouble!” someone once told him. That comment turned into the epigraph of a textbook he wrote called Conservation Aquaculture . “That’s the whole point of doing science,” he says. “It rocks the boat. It makes people think differently.” Now, he hopes that same mentality can help him nudge this unremarkable fish—and others like it—off of endangered species lists. And he aims to do so via a realization that’s only gained traction over the past decade or two: Fish can acquire the knowledge for how best to survive in a human-altered world. We just have to let them.

There may not be much that’s special about the silvery minnow, but they are tenacious. Close to 20 species of similar minnows once swam the Great Plains rivers, which includes the Rio Grande. For at least the past 50 years, the fish have suffocated under the twin pressures of drought and development. The phantom shiner and bluntnose shiner went extinct last century. The silvery minnow is hanging on.

The minnow’s endangered listing immediately sparked a long legal battle between New Mexico and the federal government. State officials worried that federal intervention to save the fish would cut the amount of water available for farms and cities, so they proposed funding silvery minnow conservation themselves. This is where the fish’s story gets interesting.

When wild fish populations dwindle, the standard recourse is to breed more in a hatchery and then restock rivers with truckloads of captive-raised fish. This is how governments replenish salmon and trout by the billions . It’s conservation as a numbers game. But over the past few decades, researchers have learned that numbers lie. Agencies spend millions of dollars breeding fish, but sometimes fewer than one in 20 hatchery fish survive after they’re released into the wild.

“We don’t raise other animals on a farm and then reintroduce them into the wild as if they are wild animals,” says Alison Hutson, who has comanaged the silvery minnow program for New Mexico’s Interstate Stream Commission with Tave since 2014, until he retired in 2021. Yet for fish, people seem to assume that they retain some innate survival skills, even in an environment that seems almost custom designed to make them duller, dumber, and unfit for the challenges of life in the wild.

In traditional hatcheries, fish are packed together and fed all the food they need, in an environment free of predators. “Your goal is to have a high survival rate,” Tave says. “And that causes all kinds of domestication issues.” The fishes’ bodies and brains change shape. Once released, they often don’t know how to eat or how to not get eaten. They have no street smarts.

The Traveling Museum of Palestinian Nature
A mobile museum brings conservation and biodiversity to rural communities in the West Bank.

A white Nissan pickup truck winds through the desert of the West Bank, inching along the 40-kilometer (25-mile) route from Bethlehem City (or Bayt Laḩm) to the Jordan Valley. It’s a tense journey, slowed by Israeli military checkpoints and a travel trailer so laden with delicate, precious things that the truck can’t go faster than 50 kilometers (31 miles) per hour. The cabinets inside are packed with scientific specimens—glass jars filled with preserved reptiles, beetles and butterflies floating on pins, mollusk shells, dried flowers and leaves. The sides of the trailer are painted with pictures of the Palestinian natural world—an eagle-owl, a griffon vulture, a mountain gazelle, a Palestine viper. Some drivers honk and wave in support as they pass.

This is the mobile museum of the Palestine Museum of Natural History, based out of Bethlehem. Although the truck’s odometer is broken, museum staff estimate that it’s traveled tens of thousands of kilometers between 2023 and 2025, teaching children about plants and wildlife in the West Bank, one of the Palestinian territories currently under Israeli occupation. Prior to this trip to the Jordan Valley in November 2025, the mobile museum had visited 114 rural communities across the West Bank.

“I don’t expect people in remote areas, Bedouin communities, or villages that are endangered by the Israeli annexation and expansion to send their people to come visit us and see natural history and [learn about] environmental issues,” says Mazin Qumsiyeh, the museum’s director and founder of the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability. “We must go to them.”

“We also tailor the exhibits relative to the area,” Qumsiyeh adds. In the Jordan Valley, for example, staff planned to teach visitors about the white storks flying over the valley on their migration to Africa.

In a faster car, without security checkpoints, the journey would take under an hour. But the biologists and museum staff members take several hours to make it to the valley: a narrow, crooked trough of sunken land running along the Jordan River to the Dead Sea. Although much of the region is hot and dry, the valley is several degrees warmer still, and significantly wetter. The river and its wetlands irrigate farmland in Syria, Israel, and Jordan—making it a strategic military buffer for Israel—and provide stopover sites for over 500 million migratory birds. The valley is also home to dozens of nomadic and permanent Palestinian communities. In one, the museum team plans to rest and have a cup of tea with the local organizers who are hosting them.

Before long, though, a crowd of schoolchildren and other villagers form around the caravan, buzzing with excitement. The staff obligingly emerge and unfold tables, bringing out boxes of scientific collections. A jar holding the coiled body of a snake yellowed by liquid preservatives gleams in the sun. The children file inside the travel trailer, and a staff member takes a taxidermied bat out of its glass enclosure and holds it up.

By bringing the museum to the most vulnerable communities, Qumsiyeh says the program challenges traditional, colonial museum models that take artifacts from oppressed places and peoples and display them for privileged patrons.

The mobile museum “then becomes an incubator for behavioral change and for revolutionary ideas: how we can stop using fossil fuels; how we can use renewable energy; how we can avoid destroying our environment with plastics, pollution, pesticides, insecticides, and things like that,” he says. Visitors to the museum have gone on to start environmental clubs at school, recycling programs, and native plant gardens.
This is the work Qumsiyeh has wanted to do all his life. His uncle, a biologist, brought a young Qumsiyeh on fieldwork trips amid the violence of his childhood: “That’s how I learned.”

In 1979, Qumsiyeh moved to the United States to study medical genetics, eventually holding teaching and research positions at Duke University in North Carolina and Yale University in Connecticut. Without USAID, Guatemala’s Forest Stewards Search for Sustainability
Communities in the Maya Biosphere Reserve are figuring out new ways to fund their work and protect their forest after losing key funding.

In the heart of Guatemala’s Maya Biosphere Reserve, day breaks over the village of Carmelita. Sunlight pokes through the swaying sapodilla trees as roosters begin to crow. Machetes in hand, residents head into the community forest.

Despite its humble visage, this little settlement in Petén, the northernmost department of Guatemala, has long been one of global conservation’s success stories. For over two decades, people in Carmelita have sustainably harvested timber, honey, and other forest products while managing nearly 55,000 hectares (approximately 136,000 acres) within the biosphere reserve.

Under a government agreement struck in 1994, large parts of Guatemala’s forests are leased to local communities through “community concessions” such as Carmelita. These custodians monetize forest products under a sustainable management plan created in conjunction with Guatemala’s national conservation agency, the National Council of Protected Areas (CONAP). The community concessions within the Maya Biosphere Reserve have collectively protected approximately 484,000 hectares (1.2 million acres) of ecologically important forest, while adjacent lands have been rapidly deforested.
“It’s like a garden,” says Jesús Barrera, Carmelita’s legal representative. “You prune it, and it becomes more beautiful. That’s how the forest is.”

Since the Maya Biosphere Reserve was established in 1990, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has been a crucial constant. It has financed everything from forestry equipment and timber mills to technical assistance for mitigating wildfires.

But the conservation story has taken a troubling political turn. A month after assuming office for the second time, U.S. President Donald Trump froze nearly all international support from USAID in February 2025.

“USAID has been an important ally of the forest model since the beginning,” says Julio Javier Madrid, coordinator of the Petén Forest Communities Association (ACOFOP). “We saw that the resources reached the places where they were needed.”

There are a dozen community concessions within the reserve that have relied on international aid for decades. With USAID’s retreat and peak fire season only months away, they face an increasingly uncertain future.
Fire has long been a part of the land within the reserve. Traditional forms of slash-and-burn agriculture have been practiced here across generations of Mayan civilizations for thousands of years.

But increasingly erratic dry seasons, coupled with the rapid expansion of cattle ranching across Petén over the past century, have caused forests to burn at alarming rates. Some 27,000 hectares (66,718 acres) of protected land burn in Guatemala every year on average. This number balloons during El Niño years.

“Fire has generated the most wear on us,” says Estuardo Miguel Julian Díaz, treasurer of one of the reserve’s community concessions, the Cruce a la Colorada Integrated Forestry Association. “It’s been difficult to control them.”

USAID helped build a network of government agencies, NGOs, and community concessions dedicated to tracking and preventing fires. This includes satellite monitoring, community fire patrols, centralized management of approved burns, and hundreds of kilometers of fire breaks. Experts say this has led to fewer fires occurring in community-managed areas in comparison to the reserve’s buffer zone.
“The withdrawal of USAID was [at] a very critical moment,” says CONAP coordinator Sergio Balan.

The funding disappeared after the reserve’s worst fire season in decades, when resources were already stretched exceptionally thin. Over 230,000 hectares (568,342 acres) of protected land burned in Petén in 2024.
“The state no longer had resources because that fire season was severe, and the available resources for fire prevention and firefighting had already been exhausted,” Balan says.

Illegal land invasions driven by cattle ranching have expanded in the reserve over the past year, particularly along what CONAP calls the “Carmelita route,” a degraded landscape under active restoration. Ranchers sometimes light fires to clear land for their animals.
The whitemargin stargazer’s ghoulish, upturned face allows the fish to bury its body in sand and nearly disappear—while watching for its next unsuspecting meal.

An orange glow appears in the darkness. It’s dim at first, then grows brighter as a group of children dressed as mermaids, bumblebees, and superheroes moves closer. Eventually, the children can make out a face, then a head, illuminated from within, perched on a neighbor’s doorstep. Like its centuries-old predecessors, the carved pumpkin is a lantern, meant to draw attention to itself and guide a path through the darkness.

In contrast, the whitemargin stargazer ( Uranoscopus sulphureus ), despite its striking resemblance to the iconic Halloween symbol, takes a different approach. One of about 50 species in the stargazer family (Uranoscopidae), the fish’s primary life strategy is to go unnoticed by both would-be predators and unwitting prey: to disappear into sandy, often shallow ocean bottoms and wait for the next life-or-death moment.

But disappearing in an environment with very little structure—nothing but sand or mud and the occasional tuft of seaweed—is no mean feat. Burial is really the only option, and for this, the stargazer is well suited. The fish’s large pectoral fins help it burrow into the ocean floor in mere seconds, and the venomous spines just above those fins deter predator attacks from above. The fringes, or cirri, around the stargazer’s mouth, which look a bit like a jack-o’-lantern’s crooked teeth, also keep sand out while the fish burrows. And unlike most fish, the stargazer’s eyes, nostrils, and mouth are positioned near the top of its head, which allows the fish to see, breathe, and be ready to snatch prey while the rest of its body remains out of sight. This unique morphology lends the fish its common—and rather poetic—name, because it’s nearly always looking up toward the night sky.

The stargazer’s ghoulish appearance, hidden watchfulness, and venomous spines are enough to send shivers through those who have seen the fish in the tropical waters of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, where it lives at depths ranging from just a couple of meters to many hundreds of meters below the surface. It has been described as a “nightmare,” and that’s from the perspective of a human, who has nothing to fear unless they should step on one. For a cardinalfish or porcelain crab, however, the stakes are much higher. One moment, you might be cruising over the seafloor looking for a bite of food. In the next, you cease to exist.
